
The output is as follows:

```
BetaRegularized(1.000000) = 1.000000
dBetaRegularized/dz(1.000000) = 0.000000
```

### 6.5.5 Gamma Derivative Function

The Gamma function is an extension of the factorial function to real and complex numbers, with its argument shifted down by 1\. For real numbers, it is defined as follows:

![$$ \Gamma (z)={\int}_0^{\infty }{x}^{z-1}{e}^{-x} dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbk.png)

The class to compute the Gamma function is `Gamma`. The class to compute the derivative function of the Gamma function is `DGamma`. Both classes inherit `evaluate(double x)` from `AbstractUnivariateRealFunction`. Their constructors do not take any argument. NM Dev has a number of implementations of the Gamma function. They have different properties in terms of accuracy and performance. The default choice is the Lanczos algorithm such that all computations are done using `double`.

Here’s an example:

```
double z = 0.5;
// Wikipedia: Lanczos approximation
Gamma G = new GammaLanczosQuick();
DGamma dG = new DGamma();
System.out.println(String.format("Gamma(%f) = %f", z, G.evaluate(z)));
System.out.println(String.format("dGamma/dz(%f) = %f", z, dG.evaluate(z)));
```

The output is as follows:

```
Gamma(0.500000) = 1.772454
dGamma/dz(0.500000) = -3.480231
```

### 6.5.6 Polynomial Derivative Function

A polynomial is not exactly a special function. We include it here because NM Dev does not use finite difference to compute the derivative function of a polynomial. There is a closed-form solution to differentiate a polynomial.

![$$ p(x)={a}_n{x}^n+\cdots {a}_1x+{a}_0 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbl.png)

![$$ \frac{dp}{dx}=n{a}_n{x}^{n-1}+\cdots {a}_2x+{a}_1 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbm.png)

The class to compute a polynomial is `Polynomial`, and its signature is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs a polynomial from an array of coefficients.
* The first/0-th entry corresponds to the xn term.
* The last/n-th entry corresponds to the constant term.
* The degree of the polynomial is n, the array length minus 1.
* 
* For example,
* 
* new Polynomial(1, -2, 3, 2)
* 
* creates an instance of {@code Polynomial} representing x3 - 2x2 + 3x + 2.
*
* @param coefficients the polynomial coefficients
*/
public Polynomial(double... coefficients)
```

The class to compute the derivative function of a polynomial is `DPolynomial`, and its signature is as follows. The derivative function of a polynomial is also a polynomial.

```
/**
* Constructs the derivative function of a {@link Polynomial}, which, again,
* is a polynomial.
*
* @param polynomial a polynomial
*/
public DPolynomial(Polynomial polynomial)
```

Here’s an example:

```
Polynomial p = new Polynomial(1, 2, 1); // x^2 + 2x + 1
Polynomial dp = new DPolynomial(p); // 2x + 2
double x = 1.;
System.out.println(String.format("dp/dx(%f) = %f", x, dp.evaluate(x)));
```

The output is as follows:

```
dp/dx(1.000000) = 4.000000
```

## 6.6 Numerical Integration

A definite integral is the (signed) area under a curve or a function *f*(*x*), called the integrand, between two points [*a*, *b*] in the real line. It is defined as follows:

![$$ I={\int}_a^bf(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbn.png)

The symbol *dx*, called the differential of the variable *x*, indicates that the variable of integration is *x*. It means a small change in *x* as in differentiation. Integration is the process of computing the value of a definite integral. The first fundamental theorem of calculus says that the derivative of an integral is the integrand. So, we sometimes call the integral the anti-derivative of a function. See Figure [6-10](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig10).

![$$ f(x)=\frac{d}{dx}{\int}_0^xf(t) dt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbo.png)

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig10_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig10_HTML.png)

Figure 6-10

Integral as the signed area under curve

Riemann gave the first rigorous definition of an integral. The basic idea of the Riemann integral is to partition the area into many rectangles to approximate the area and then to sum them up (hence integration). By taking better and better approximations, say infinitely many infinitesimally small rectangles, we can say that “in the limit” we get exactly the area under the curve. Figure [6-11](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig11) shows a sequence of Riemann sums over a regular partition of an interval. The number on top is the total area of the rectangles, which converges to the integral of the function.

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig11_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig11_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-11

A sequence of Riemann sums

Mathematically, a partition of an interval [*a*, *b*] is a finite sequence of points.

![$$ a={x}_0&lt;{x}_1&lt;\cdots {x}_n=b $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbp.png)

There is a distinguished point *t*[*i*] ∈ [*x*[*i*], *x*[*i* + 1]] in each subinterval to determine the height of the rectangle *f*(*t*[*i*]). The rectangle area size is therefore *f*(*t*[*i*])(*x*[*i* + 1] − *x*[*i*]). The Riemann sum of *f* with respect to the partition is defined as the sum of all the rectangles.

![$$ {S}_n=\sum \limits_{i=0}^{n-1}f\left({t}_i\right)\left({x}_{i+1}-{x}_i\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbq.png)

When we take the limit that *n* goes to infinity, the Riemann sum becomes the integral value.

![$$ I=\underset{n\to \infty }{\lim }{S}_n $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbr.png)

Numerical integration is a technique that approximates a definite integral using a similar partitioning concept: using a weighted average approximation of the limited sample values of the integrand to replace the value of the function. Numerical integration is important because it is (often) not possible to find the (closed-form) antiderivative analytically. Even if antiderivatives exist, they may not be easy to compute because they cannot be composed of elementary functions. It is so much easier to compute a numerical approximation than the antiderivative in terms of special functions or infinite series. Moreover, the integrand may be known only at certain points, such as obtained by sampling. Some embedded systems and other computer applications may need numerical integration for this reason.

Traditionally, the mathematics of finding the size of an area is called the quadrature. It is now a synonym for integration but less popularly used. The numerical integration formulas are still called numerical quadrature formulas. There are many ways to do numerical integration. They differ by how many partitions they divide the interval into, whether the partitions are equally spaced, how we choose the distinguished points, whether it is open (not using endpoints) or closed (using endpoints), and how we do extrapolation (or not). This chapter can only scratch the surface to introduce some of the most basic variants.

## 6.7 The Newton-Cotes Family

The Newton-Cotes formulas, also called the Newton-Cotes quadrature rules or simply Newton-Cotes rules, are a group of formulas for numerical integration (also called a quadrature) based on evaluating an integrand at equally spaced points. They are named after Isaac Newton and Roger Cotes. Newton-Cotes formulas can be useful if the values of the integrand at equally spaced points are available. If it is possible to use a different set (of possibly not equally spaced) points, then other methods such as Gaussian quadrature are probably more accurate. There are many derivations of the Newton-Cotes formulas. Two of the most famous ones are the trapezoidal quadrature and the Simpson quadrature formulas.

### 6.7.1 The Trapezoidal Quadrature Formula

The trapezoidal formula works by replacing the function using a straight line, essentially approximating the region under the function as a trapezoid and calculating its area. See Figure [6-12](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig12).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig12_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig12_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-12

The trapezoidal formula

The line equation passing through the two points *a* and *b* is as follows:

![$$ {L}_1(x)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\left(x-a\right)+f(a) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbs.png)

The area under the line is the area of the trapezoidal that is simply multiplying the sum of the bases (the parallel sides) by the height (the perpendicular distance between the bases) and then dividing by 2\. We can also do a proper integration to get the same result.

Replacing *f*(*x*) with *L*[1](*x*), we have this:

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx\approx {\int}_a^b{L}_1(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbt.png)

![$$ ={\int}_a^b\left[\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\left(x-a\right)+f(a)\right] dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbu.png)

![$$ =\frac{f(a)+f(b)}{2}\left(b-a\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbv.png)

For a function *f*(*x*) and an interval [*a*, *b*], we can divide the interval into *N* subintervals. Then we apply this trapezoidal rule to each subinterval and sum them up.

Let

![$$ \Delta x=\frac{b-a}{N} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbw.png)

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx\approx \frac{\Delta x}{2}\sum \limits_{k=1}^N\left(f\left({x}_{k-1}\right)+f\left({x}_k\right)\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbx.png)

It can be proved that, assuming *f*^(′′)(*x*) exists and is continuous on [*a*, *b*], the error from using the trapezoidal rule is as follows for some *ξ* ∈ [*a*, *b*]:

![$$ \varepsilon =-\frac{{\left(b-a\right)}^3}{12N}{f}^{\prime \prime}\left(\xi \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equby.png)

In NM Dev, the class to do the trapezoidal integration is `Trapezoidal`. The following example solves the problem in Figure [6-12](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig12):

```
final UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return -(x * x - 4 * x + 6); // -(x^2 - 4x + 6)
}
};
// the limit
double a = 0., b = 4.;
// an integrator using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // precision, max number of iterations
// the integration
double I = integrator.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,4] f(x) dx = -13.333333
```

The class signature for `Trapezoidal` is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs an integrator that implements the Trapezoidal rule.
*
* @param precision     the convergence threshold
* @param maxIterations the maximum number of iterations
*/
public Trapezoidal(double precision, int maxIterations)
```

In NM Dev, all implementations of an integrator (algorithm) inherit from this class `Integrator`. They all call `integrate` to do the job.

```
/**
* Integrate function f from a to b,
* \[
* \int_a^b\! f(x)\, dx
* \]
*
* @param f a univariate function
* @param a the lower limit
* @param b the upper limit
* @return \(\int_a^b\! f(x)\, dx\)
*/
public double integrate(UnivariateRealFunction f, double a, double b);
```

### 6.7.2 The Simpson Quadrature Formula

The Simpson formula , instead of replacing the function by a line, replaces *f*(*x*) by a quadratic function or a parabola. The interval is divided into two partitions giving three points: *a*, *b*, and a midpoint ![$$ m=\frac{a+b}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq7.png). The quadratic function is as follows:

![$$ {L}_2(x)= $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equbz.png)

![$$ \frac{\left(x-m\right)\left(x-b\right)}{\left(a-m\right)\left(a-b\right)}f(a)+\frac{\left(x-a\right)\left(x-b\right)}{\left(m-a\right)\left(m-b\right)}f(m)+\frac{\left(x-m\right)\left(x-a\right)}{\left(b-m\right)\left(b-a\right)}f(b) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equca.png)

From a geometrical point of view, the Simpson formula calculates the area of the curved trapezoid surrounded by a parabola to approximate the area enclosed by *f*(*x*). See Figure [6-13](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig13).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig13_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig13_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-13

The Simpson formula

Replacing *f*(*x*) with *L*[2](*x*), we have this:

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx\approx {\int}_a^b{L}_2(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcb.png)

![$$ =\frac{b-a}{6}\left[f(a)+4f\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)+f(b)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcc.png)

![$$ =\frac{h}{3}\left[f(a)+4f\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)+f(b)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcd.png)

![$$ h=\frac{b-a}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq8.png) is the step size in each partition. Because of the ![$$ \frac{1}{3} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq9.png) in the formula, this Simpson rule is often called Simpson’s 1/3 rule.

For a function *f*(*x*) and an interval [*a*, *b*], we can divide the interval into *N* subintervals. Then we apply this Simpson rule to each subinterval and the sum them up. We have the following:

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx\approx \frac{h}{3}\sum \limits_{j=1}^{N/2}\left[f\left({x}_{2j-2}\right)+4f\left({x}_{2j-1}\right)+f\left({x}_{2j}\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equce.png)

The Simpson rule is expected to improve on the trapezoidal rule for functions that are twice continuously differentiable. However, for rougher functions, the trapezoidal rule is likely to be more preferable. It can be proved that, assuming the fourth-order derivative *f*^((4))(*x*) exists and is continuous on [*a*, *b*], the error from using Simpson’s 1/3 rule is as follows for some *ξ* ∈ [*a*, *b*]:

![$$ \varepsilon =-\frac{h^4}{180}\left(b-a\right){f}^{(4)}\left(\xi \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcf.png)

In NM Dev, the class to do Simpson’s 1/3 integration is `Trapezoidal`. The following example solves the problem in Figure [6-12](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig12):

```
final UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return -(x * x - 4 * x + 6); // -(x^2 - 4x + 6)
}
};
// the limit
double a = 0., b = 4.;
// an integrator using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // precision, max number of iterations
// the integration
double I = integrator.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,4] f(x) dx = -13.333333
```

The class signature for `Simpson` is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs an integrator that implements Simpson's rule.
*
* @param precision     the convergence threshold
* @param maxIterations the maximum number of iterations
*/
public Simpson(double precision, int maxIterations)
```

### 6.7.3 The Newton-Cotes Quadrature Formulas

It is conceivable that one can divide the interval [*a*, *b*] into more than one partition (as in the case of the trapezoidal rule) or more than two partitions (as in the case of the Simpson’s rule). One can divide it into *n* intervals. One can also use a closed formula where the endpoints *a* and *b* are used, or an open formula where the endpoints are not used because *f*(*a*) and *f*(*b*) may not exist. The Newton-Cotes formula is such a generalization. It divides the interval [*a*, *b*] into *n* equal partitions. For a closed formula, the equally spaced points are as follows:

*x*[*i*] = *a* + *ih*, ![$$ h=\frac{b-a}{n} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq10.png)

For an open formula, the equally spaced points are as follows:

*x*[*i*] = *a* + (*i* + 1)*h*, ![$$ h=\frac{b-a}{n+2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq11.png)

For the closed formula, an *n*-th degree difference polynomial can be constructed, as shown here:

![$$ {L}_n(x)={\sum}_{k=0}^n\frac{w(x)}{\left(x-{x}_k\right){w}^{\prime}\left({x}_k\right)}f\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcg.png)

where *w*(*x*) = (*x* − *x*[0])(*x* − *x*[1])⋯(*x* − *x*[*n*]).

Replacing *f*(*x*) with *L*[*n*](*x*), we have the following:

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx\approx {\int}_a^b{L}_n(x) dx={\int}_a^b\left({\sum}_{k=0}^n\frac{w(x)}{\left(x-{x}_k\right){w}^{\prime}\left({x}_k\right)}f\left({x}_k\right)\right) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equch.png)

![$$ ={\sum}_{i=0}^n\left({\int}_a^b\frac{w(x)}{\left(x-{x}_k\right){w}^{\prime}\left({x}_k\right)} dx\right)f\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equci.png)

![$$ ={\sum}_{i=0}^n{A}_kf\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcj.png)

where the coefficients ![$$ {A}_k={\int}_a^b\frac{w(x)}{\left(x-{x}_k\right){w}^{\prime}\left({x}_k\right)} dx. $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq12.png)

This formula is called the Newton-Cotes formula. The coefficients are called the Newton-Cotes coefficients. To use the formula, we need to calculate the coefficients *A*[*k*]. Substitute *x* = *a* + *th*. We have the following:

![$$ w(x)=w\left(a+ th\right)={h}^{n+1}t\left(t-1\right)\cdots \left(t-n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equck.png)

![$$ {w}^{\prime }(x)={h}^n{\left(-1\right)}^{n-1}\left(k!\right)\left(n-k\right)! $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcl.png)

![$$ {A}_k={\int}_a^b\frac{w(x)}{\left(x-{x}_k\right){w}^{\prime}\left({x}_k\right)} dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcm.png)

![$$ ={\int}_0^n\frac{h^{n+1}t\left(t-1\right)\cdots \left(t-n\right)}{h^n{\left(-1\right)}^{n-1}\left(k!\right)\left(n-k\right)!h\left(t-k\right)} hdt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcn.png)

Let

![$$ {C}_k^{(n)}=\frac{{\left(-1\right)}^{n-k}}{n\left(k!\right)\left(n-k\right)!}{\int}_0^n\frac{t\left(t-1\right)\cdots \left(t-n\right)}{\left(t-k\right)} dt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equco.png)

So

![$$ {A}_k=\left(b-a\right){C}_k^{(n)} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcp.png)

We see that *A*[*k*] is a constant that depends only on the interval [*a*, *b*] and the number of partitions *n* but not on the function. The Newton-Cotes coefficients can therefore be computed in advance.

The trapezoidal formula and the Simpson formula are special cases of the Newton-Cotes formula. When *n* = 1, the Newton-Cotes formula is as follows:

![$$ {L}_1(x)=\frac{b-a}{2}\left[f(a)+f(b)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcq.png)

This is the trapezoidal formula.

When *n* = 2, the Newton-Cotes formula is as follows:

![$$ {L}_2(x)=\frac{b-a}{6}\left[f(a)+4f\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)+f(b)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcr.png)

This is the Simpson formula.

When *n* = 4, the Newton-Cotes formula is as follows:

![$$ C=\frac{b-a}{90}\left[7f\left({x}_0\right)+32f\left({x}_1\right)+12f\left({x}_2\right)+32f\left({x}_3\right)+7f\left({x}_4\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcs.png)

And *x*[*i*] = *a* + *kh* (*k* = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4) and ![$$ h=\frac{b-a}{4} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq13.png). See Figure [6-14](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig14).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig14_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig14_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-14

The Newton-Cotes formula for n=2 and n = 4

Algebraic accuracy is a way of measuring how good an approximation of a numerical integration formula is. Note that the Newton-Cotes coefficient *A*[*k*] depends on *n* but not on the integrand function itself. For *n* = 1, the trapezoidal formula is a polynomial of degree 1\. If *f*(*x*) in the Newton-Cotes formula is a polynomial with a degree no higher than *n*, then the equal sign holds.

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx\approx {\sum}_{k=0}^n{A}_kf\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equct.png)

If *f*(*x*) is a polynomial of degree *n* + 1, the right-hand side is only an approximation. The quadrature formula is said to have an *n*-degree algebraic accuracy.

For *n* = 1, the trapezoidal quadrature rule has this error and is said to have the primary algebraic precision.

![$$ \varepsilon =-\frac{{\left(b-a\right)}^3}{12N}{f}^{\prime \prime}\left(\xi \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq14.png), *a* ≤ *ξ* ≤ *b*

For *n* = 2, the Simpson quadrature rule has this error and is said to have cubic algebraic precision.

![$$ \varepsilon =-\frac{h^4}{180}\left(b-a\right){f}^{(4)}\left(\xi \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq15.png), *a* ≤ *ξ* ≤ *b*

For a general *n*, the error term is as follows:

![$$ \varepsilon =\frac{f^{\left(n+1\right)}\left(\xi \right)}{\left(n+1\right)!}w(x) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq16.png), *a* ≤ *ξ* ≤ *b*

If *f*(*x*) is a polynomial of degree *n*, then *f*^((*n* + 1))(*x*) = 0\. So, the error *ε* = 0\. The algebraic accuracy of the Newton-Cotes quadrature formula is at least *n*. There is a theorem that says when *n* is odd, the algebraic accuracy is *n*. When *n* is even, the algebraic accuracy is *n* + 1\. For instance, the Simpson formula has an algebraic accuracy of 3 for *n* = 2\. For *n* = 4, the algebraic accuracy is 5.

Assuming that the rounding error of *f*(*x*[*i*]) (*x*[*i*] are the grid points) is ![$$ {\varepsilon}_i,{\varepsilon}_{max}=\underset{0\le i\le n}{\mathit{\max}}\mid {\varepsilon}_i\mid $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq17.png), the error of the Newton-Cotes formula is as follows:

![$$ \varepsilon =\left|b-a\right|\cdotp \left|{\sum}_{i=0}^n{C}_i^{(n)}{\varepsilon}_i\right|\le \mid \left(b-a\right)\mid \cdotp {\varepsilon}_{max}\cdotp \mid {\sum}_{i=0}^n{C}_i^{(n)}\mid $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcu.png)

The last term, ![$$ {\sum}_{i=0}^n\mid {C}_i^{(n)}\mid $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq18.png), increases with *n*. This will cause the error of the approximation to increase, so the Newton-Cotes formula is unstable for big *n*. Therefore, in practice the Newton-Cotes formula is rarely used for *n* ≥ 8.

Consider this example of integrating the following function:

![$$ I={\int}_0^1 ydx={\int}_0^1\frac{4}{1+{x}^2} dx=\pi $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcv.png)

See Figure [6-15](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig15).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig15_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig15_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-15

A definite integral for π

Using the trapezoid formula, we have the following:

![$$ {\int}_0^1 ydx\approx \frac{1-0}{2}\left[\frac{4}{1+1}+\frac{4}{1+0}\right]=3 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcw.png)

See Figure [6-16](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig16).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig16_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig16_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-16

The trapezoid formula for π

Using the Simpson formula, we have the following:

![$$ {\int}_0^1 ydx\approx \frac{1-0}{6}\left[\frac{4}{1+1}+4\frac{4}{1+\frac{1}{4}}+\frac{4}{1+0}\right]\approx 3.1333 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcx.png)

See Figure [6-17](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig17) and Figure [6-18](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig18).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig18_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig18_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-18

Simpson’s formula for π

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig17_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig17_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-17

Simpson’s formula for π

Using the Newton-Cotes formula with *n* = 4, we have the following:

![$$ {x}_0=0,{x}_1=0.2500,{x}_2=0.5000,{x}_3=0.7500,{x}_4=1.0000 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcy.png)

![$$ {\int}_0^1 ydx\approx \frac{b-a}{90}\left[7f\left({x}_0\right)+32f\left({x}_1\right)+12f\left({x}_2\right)+32f\left({x}_3\right)+7f\left({x}_4\right)\right]\approx 3.1421 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equcz.png)

See Figure [6-19](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig19) and Figure [6-20](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig20).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig20_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig20_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-20

The Newton-Cotes formula with n=4 for π

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig19_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig19_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-19

The Newton-Cotes formula with n=4 for π

The following NM Dev code solves this example:

```
System.out.println("integrate using the Newton-Cotes formulas");
final UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return 4\. / (1\. + x * x); // 4/(1+x^2)
}
};
// the limit
double a = 0., b = 1.;
Integrator integrator1 = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator2 = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator3 = new NewtonCotes(3, Type.CLOSED, 1e-8, 20); // using the Newton-Cotes rule
Integrator integrator4 = new NewtonCotes(3, Type.OPEN, 1e-8, 20); // using the Newton-Cotes rule
// the integrations
double I1 = integrator1.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f", a, b, I1));
double I2 = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f", a, b, I2));
double I3 = integrator3.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f", a, b, I3));
double I4 = integrator4.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f", a, b, I4));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = 3.1415926436556850, using the trapezoidal rule
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = 3.1415926535528365, using the Simpson rule
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = 3.1415926497180000, using the Newton-Cotes closed rule
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = 3.1415926674370604, using using the Newton-Cotes open rule
```

The signature for the class `NewtonCotes` is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs an instance of the Newton-Cotes quadrature.
*
* @param rate          the rate of further sub-dividing an integral
*                      interval. For example, when {@code rate = 2}, we
*                      divide [xi, xi+1] into
*                      two equal length intervals. This is equivalent to
*                      the Trapezoidal rule.
* @param type          specifying whether to use CLOSED or OPEN formula
* @param precision     the precision required, e.g., {@code 1e-8}
* @param maxIterations the maximum number of iterations
*/
public NewtonCotes(int rate, Type type, double precision, int maxIterations)
```

The accuracy and performance of an integration depend not only on which quadrature formula to use but also on the integrand function itself. In general, the trapezoidal formula is not as accurate as the Simpson formula. The low-order Newton-Cotes formulas are simple to compute, are convenient to use, and have a high degree of accuracy. On the other hand, the higher-order Newton-Cotes formulas are not only complicated to calculate but also have poor stability. So, they are rarely used. In practice, we in general prefer low-order formulas like the Simpson rule.

## 6.8 Romberg Integration

The Romberg quadrature formula is also called the successive half-acceleration method. It is based on the relationship between the trapezoidal formula, the Simpson formula, and the higher-order Newton-Cotes formula to construct a method to accelerate the calculation of integral. The Romberg algorithm is an extrapolation method of combining the previous approximations to generate more accurate approximations in the process of successively dividing the integration interval into half. It improves the accuracy of the integral without increasing the amount of calculation.

According to the error estimation of the trapezoid rule, it can be seen that the truncation error of the integral (approximation) value *T*[*n*] is roughly proportional to *h*². So, when the step size is divided by two doubling the number of subintervals, the truncation error, *I* − *T*[*n*], will be reduced to ![$$ \frac{1}{4} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq19.png) of the original error. That is,

![$$ \frac{I-{T}_{2n}}{I-{T}_n}\approx \frac{1}{4} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equda.png)

We can rearrange the terms to get the following:

![$$ I-{T}_{2n}\approx \frac{1}{3}\left({T}_{2n}-{T}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdb.png)

It can be seen that as long as the two successive integral values *T*[*n*] and *T*[2*n*] before and after the further interval division are close enough, the error of the *T*[2*n*] calculation result will be small. The error of *T*[2*n*] is roughly equal to ![$$ \frac{1}{3}\left({T}_{2n}-{T}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq20.png). We can use this error to compensate for *T*[2*n*] to get an even better estimation. That is, a more accurate approximation is as follows:

![$$ \overline{T}={T}_{2n}+\frac{1}{3}\left({T}_{2n}-{T}_n\right)=\frac{4}{3}{T}_{2n}-\frac{1}{3}{T}_n $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdc.png)

That is to say, we linearly combine the two integral values *T*[*n*] and *T*[2*n*] computed using the trapezoid rule to get a more accurate approximation. We can go further than this.

We can generate a Simpson sequence, ![$$ \left\{{S}_{2^k}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq21.png), by linearly combining the values from the trapezoidal sequence ![$$ \left\{{T}_{2^k}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq22.png). The Simpson sequence has a faster convergence rate than that of the trapezoidal sequence.

![$$ \left\{{S}_{2^k}\right\}:{S}_1,{S}_2,{S}_4\dots $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdd.png)

![$$ {S}_n=\overline{T}=\frac{4}{3}{T}_{2n}-\frac{1}{3}{T}_n=\frac{4{T}_{2n}-{T}_n}{4-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equde.png)

Using a similar calculation, it can be shown that

![$$ I\approx {S}_{2n}+\frac{1}{15}\left({S}_{2n}-{S}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdf.png)

We can go further by linearly combining the values from the Simpson sequence to produce a Cotes sequence ![$$ \left\{{C}_{2^k}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq23.png) with a faster convergence rate. It can be shown that

![$$ {C}_{2n}=\frac{16}{15}{S}_{2n}-\frac{1}{15}{S}_n=\frac{4^2{S}_{2n}-{S}_n}{4^2-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdg.png)

Using a similar calculation, it can be shown that

![$$ I\approx {C}_{2n}+\frac{1}{63}\left({C}_{2n}-{C}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdh.png)

We can go even further by linearly combining the values from the Cotes sequence to produce a Romberg sequence ![$$ \left\{{R}_{2^k}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq24.png) with an even faster convergence rate.

![$$ \left\{{R}_{2^k}\right\}:{R}_1,{R}_2,{R}_4\dots $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdi.png)

![$$ {R}_n=\frac{64}{63}{C}_{2n}-\frac{1}{63}{C}_n=\frac{4^3{C}_{2n}-{C}_n}{4^3-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdj.png)

By using the acceleration formula in the process of variable step size, we gradually process the rough trapezoidal values *T*[*n*] into the fine Simpson values *S*[*n*], then into the finer Cotes values *C*[*n*], and then into the Romberg values *R*[*n*] with the highest precision. Figure [6-21](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig21) illustrates the progression sequence.

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig21_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig21_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-21

The Romberg formula

Let’s repeat the example of calculating *π* using the integral in Section 6.7.3\. The following is the sequence of trapezoidal values, Simpson values, Cotes values, and the Romberg values produced. See Figure [6-22](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig22).

![$$ I={\int}_0^1 ydx={\int}_0^1\frac{4}{1+{x}^2} dx=\pi $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdk.png)

![$$ f(x)=\frac{4}{1+{x}^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdl.png)

![$$ {T}_1=\frac{1}{2}\left[f(0)+f(1)\right]=3 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdm.png)

![$$ {T}_2=\frac{1}{2}{T}_1+\frac{1}{2}f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=3.1 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdn.png)

![$$ {S}_1=\frac{4}{3}{T}_2-\frac{1}{3}{T}_1=3.13333 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdo.png)

![$$ {T}_4=\frac{1}{2}{T}_2+\frac{1}{4}\left[f\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)+f\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\right]=3.131177 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdp.png)

![$$ {S}_2=\frac{4}{3}{T}_4-\frac{1}{3}{T}_2=3.141569 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdq.png)

![$$ {T}_8=\frac{1}{2}{T}_4+\frac{1}{8}\left[f\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)+f\left(\frac{3}{8}\right)+f\left(\frac{5}{8}\right)+f\left(\frac{7}{8}\right)\right]=3.138989 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdr.png)

![$$ {S}_4=\frac{8}{3}{T}_8-\frac{1}{3}{T}_4=3.141593 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equds.png)

![$$ {C}_1=\frac{16}{15}{S}_2-\frac{1}{15}{S}_1=3.142118 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdt.png)

![$$ {C}_2=\frac{16}{15}{S}_4-\frac{1}{15}{S}_2=3.1415946 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdu.png)

![$$ {R}_1=\frac{64}{63}{C}_2-\frac{1}{63}{C}_1=3.141586292 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdv.png)

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig22_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig22_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-22

The Romberg integral

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig23_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig23_HTML.png)

Figure 6-23

A Romberg integral

In NM Dev, the class to do Romberg integration is `Romberg`. The following code computes this integral value using Romberg integration.

```
final UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return exp(2\. * x) - 4\. * x - 7.;
}
};
IterativeIntegrator integrator1 = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator2 = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator3 = new Romberg(integrator1);
// the limit
double a = 0., b = 1.;
// the integrations
double I1 = integrator1.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the trapezoidal rule", a, b, I1));
double I2 = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Simpson rule", a, b, I2));
double I3 = integrator3.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Romberg formula", a, b, I3));
```

The output is:

```
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = -5.8054719346672840, using the trapezoidal rule
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = -5.8054719494768790, using the Simpson rule
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = -5.8054719505327520, using the Romberg formula
```

The signature is:

```
/**
* Extends an integrator using Romberg’s method.
*
* @param integrator an iterative integrator that must do at least 2
*                   iterations
*/
public Romberg(IterativeIntegrator integrator)
```

## 6.9 Gauss Quadrature

The Newton-Cotes family of quadrature formulas introduced in the previous section is characterized by the *n* + 1 nodes (*x*[0], *x*[1], ⋯, *x*[*n*]) being equidistant or equally spaced. Consequently, their quadrature formulas are easy to construct. On the other hand, it limits the accuracy of those formulas. When *n* is odd, the algebraic accuracy is *n*. When *n* is even, the algebraic accuracy is *n* + 1\. Can the algebraic accuracy be bigger if those *n* + 1 nodes are properly selected, i.e., not necessarily equally spaced? It can be shown that the algebraic accuracy can be up to 2*n* + 1 if we choose the nodes right.

From Figure [6-24](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig24), we see that the error of integration using the trapezoidal rule is relatively large. If we can position our nodes wisely as in Figure [6-25](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig25), we can use another line approximation that balances out the positive and negative errors.

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig25_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig25_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-25

Gauss quadrature versus trapezoidal rule

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig24_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig24_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-24

Gauss quadrature versus trapezoidal rule

Consider an example to integrate this polynomial:

![$$ f(x)=7{x}^3-8{x}^2-3x+3 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdw.png)

The integral value is as follows:

![$$ {\int}_{-1}^1\left(7{x}^3-8{x}^2-3x+3\right) dx=\frac{2}{3} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdx.png)

See Figure [6-26](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig26).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig26_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig26_HTML.png)

Figure 6-26

Gauss quadrature versus trapezoidal rule

Using the trapezoidal rule, the orange line approximates the polynomial and gives the following:

![$$ f\left(-1\right)+f(1)=-10 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdy.png)

The two-point Gaussian quadrature rule uses the dashed black line to approximate the polynomial. It gives the exact result. The green region has the same area size as the sum of the red regions.

![$$ f\left(-\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\right)+f\left(\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\right)=\frac{2}{3} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equdz.png)

In general, the Gauss quadrature formula (note that we change the symbol from *A*[*k*] to *w*[*k*] because the coefficients or weights are now computed differently) on an integral of this form

![$$ {\int}_a^b\rho (x)f(x) dx\approx \sum \limits_{k=0}^n{w}_kf\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equea.png)

can achieve the algebraic accuracy of at least *n* and up to 2*n* + 1, if we can choose the right set of nodes. The nodes, {*x*[*k*]}, are called the Gauss points, and the coefficients, {*w*[*k*]}, are called the Gauss coefficients. Both the nodes and the coefficients do not depend on the integrand function. The nodes, {*x*[*k*]}, are computed from the roots of a polynomial, depending on the form of the integrand, or *ρ*(*x*).

### 6.9.1 Gauss-Legendre Quadrature Formula

The Gauss-Legendre quadrature formula solves the integral of the following form for *ρ*(*x*) = 1.

![$$ {\int}_{-1}^1\rho (x)f(x) dx\approx \sum \limits_{k=0}^n{w}_kf\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equeb.png)

The Gauss nodes are the roots of the Legendre polynomial *P*[*n*](*x*).

*P*[*n*](*x*) is a polynomial of degree *n* such that they are orthogonal. Two polynomials or functions that are orthogonal if and only if they satisfy:

![$$ {\int}_{-1}^1{P}_m(x){P}_n(x) dx=0 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq25.png), if *n* ≠ *m*

Figure [6-27](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig27) shows the first 11 Legendre polynomials (for *n* = 0, ⋯, 10).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig27_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig27_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-27

The first 11 Legendre polynomials

We plot the first six of them in Figure [6-28](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig28).

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig28_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig28_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-28

The first six Legendre polynomials

The weights {*w*[*k*]} are as follows:

![$$ {w}_k=\frac{2}{\left(1-{x}_k^2\right){\left[{P}_n^{\prime}\left({x}_k\right)\right]}^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equec.png)

Some low-order quadrature rules are tabulated in Figure [6-29](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig29) over interval [−1, 1].

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig29_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig29_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-29

Low-order Gauss-Legendre quadrature rules

With the Gauss nodes and Gauss weights, the Gauss-Legendre quadrature formula is as follows:

![$$ {\int}_{-1}^1f(x) dx\approx \sum \limits_{k=0}^n{w}_kf\left({x}_k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equed.png)

In fact, for functions that are polynomials with a degree up to 2*n* + 1, the equation is exact.

In NM Dev, the class to do Gauss-Legendre quadrature is `GaussLegendreQuadrature`. The following code computes this integral:

![$$ I={\int}_{-1}^1\left({x}^4+{x}^2+x\right) dx=2 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equee.png)

```
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return 4 * x * x * x + 2 * x + 1; // x^4 + x^2 + x
}
};
// the integrators
Integrator integrator1 = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator2 = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator3 = new GaussLegendreQuadrature(2);
// the limits
double a = -1., b = 1.;
// the integrations
double I1 = integrator1.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the trapezoidal rule", a, b, I1));
double I2 = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Simpson rule", a, b, I2));
double I3 = integrator3.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Gauss Legendre quadrature", a, b, I3));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[-1,1] f(x) dx = 2.0000000000000000, using the trapezoidal rule
S_[-1,1] f(x) dx = 2.0000000000000000, using the Simpson rule
S_[-1,1] f(x) dx = 2.0000000000000000, using the Gauss Legendre quadrature
```

The class signature of `GaussLegendreQuadrature` is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs an integrator of order n.
*
* @param n the number of points in the quadrature rule
*/
public GaussLegendreQuadrature(final int n)
```

### 6.9.2 Gauss-Laguerre Quadrature Formula

The Gauss-Laguerre quadrature formula numerically computes the integrals of this form.

![$$ {\int}_0^{\infty }{e}^{-x}f(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equef.png)

The Gauss nodes, {*x*[*k*]}, are the roots of the Laguerre polynomials *L*[*n*](*x*).

Figure [6-30](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig30) shows the first few Laguerre polynomials.

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig30_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig30_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-30

Laguerre polynomials

The Gauss coefficients, {*w*[*k*]}, are as follows:

![$$ {w}_k=\frac{x_k}{{\left(n+1\right)}^2{\left[{L}_{n+1}\left({x}_k\right)\right]}^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equeg.png)

In NM Dev, the class to do Gauss-Laguerre quadrature is `GaussLaguerreQuadrature`. The following code computes this integral:

![$$ I={\int}_0^{\infty }{e}^{-x}\left({x}^2+2x+1\right) dx=5 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equeh.png)

```
final Polynomial poly = new Polynomial(1, 2, 1); // x^2 + 2x + 1
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return exp(-x) * poly.evaluate(x); // e^-x * (x^2 + 2x + 1)
}
};
// the integrators
Integrator integrator1 = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator2 = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator3 = new GaussLaguerreQuadrature(2, 1e-8);
// the limits
double a = 0., b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
// the integrations
double I1 = integrator1.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the trapezoidal rule", a, b, I1));
double I2 = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Simpson rule", a, b, I2));
double I3 = integrator3.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Gauss Laguerre quadrature", a, b, I3));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,Infinity] f(x) dx = NaN, using the trapezoidal rule
S_[0,Infinity] f(x) dx = NaN, using the Simpson rule
S_[0,Infinity] f(x) dx = 5.0000000000000000, using the Gauss Laguerre quadrature
```

It is interesting to note that neither the trapezoidal nor the Simpson rule can compute this (improper) integral of which one of the limit is positive infinity. We can’t divide the half real-life [0, ∞] into partitions.

The class signature of `GaussLaguerreQuadrature` is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs an integrator of order n.
*
* @param n         the number of points in the quadrature rule
* @param precision the precision of the estimates of the coefficients
*/
public GaussLaguerreQuadrature(final int n, final double precision)
```

### 6.9.3 Gauss-Hermite Quadrature Formula

The Gauss-Hermite quadrature formula numerically computes the integrals of this form:

![$$ {\int}_{-\infty}^{\infty }{e}^{-{x}^2}f(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equei.png)

The Gauss nodes, {*x*[*k*]}, are the roots of the physicists’ version of Hermite polynomials *H*[*n*](*x*).

Figure [6-31](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig31) and Figure [6-32](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Fig32) show the first few Hermite polynomials.

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig32_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig32_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-32

The first six Hermite polynomials

![../images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig31_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Fig31_HTML.jpg)

Figure 6-31

The first 10 Hermite polynomials

The Gauss coefficients, {*w*[*k*]}, are as follows:

![$$ {w}_k=\frac{2^{n-1}n!\sqrt{\pi }}{n^2{\left[{H}_{n-1}\left({x}_k\right)\right]}^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equej.png)

In NM Dev, the class to do Gauss-Hermite quadrature is `GaussHermiteQuadrature`. The following code computes this integral:

![$$ I={\int}_0^{\infty }{e}^{-{x}^2}\left({x}^2+2x+1\right) dx=\frac{3\sqrt{\pi }}{2}\approx 2.658681 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equek.png)

```
final Polynomial poly = new Polynomial(1, 2, 1); // x^2 + 2x + 1
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return exp(-(x * x)) * poly.evaluate(x); // e^(-x^2) * (x^2 + 2x + 1)
}
};
// the integrators
Integrator integrator1 = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator2 = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator3 = new GaussHermiteQuadrature(2);
// the limits
double a = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
// the integrations
double I1 = integrator1.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the trapezoidal rule", a, b, I1));
double I2 = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Simpson rule", a, b, I2));
double I3 = integrator3.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Gauss Hermite quadrature", a, b, I3));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[-Infinity,Infinity] f(x) dx = NaN, using the trapezoidal rule
S_[-Infinity,Infinity] f(x) dx = NaN, using the Simpson rule
S_[-Infinity,Infinity] f(x) dx = 2.6586807763582730, using the Gauss Hermite quadrature
```

Note that neither the trapezoidal nor the Simpson rule can compute this (improper) integral of which both limits are infinity. We can’t divide the real-line [−∞, ∞] into partitions.

The class signature of `GaussHermiteQuadrature` is as follows:

```
/**
* Constructs an integrator of order n.
*
* @param n the number of points in the quadrature rule
*/
public GaussHermiteQuadrature(final int n)
```

### 6.9.4 Gauss-Chebyshev Quadrature Formula

The Gauss-Chebyshev quadrature formula numerically computes the integrals of this form:

![$$ {\int}_{-1}^1\frac{f(x)}{\sqrt{1-{x}^2}} dx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equel.png)

The Gauss nodes, {*x*[*k*]}, are as follows:

![$$ {x}_k=\cos \left(\frac{2i-1}{2n}\pi \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equem.png)

The Gauss coefficients, {*w*[*k*]}, are as follows:

![$$ {w}_k=\frac{\pi }{n} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equen.png)

In NM Dev, the class to do Gauss-Chebyshev quadrature is `GaussChebyshevQuadrature`. The following code computes this integral:

![$$ I={\int}_{-1}^1\frac{x^2+2x+1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^2}} dx=\frac{3\pi }{2}\approx 4.712389 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equeo.png)

```
final Polynomial poly = new Polynomial(1, 2, 1); // x^2 + 2x + 1
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
// second order polynomial divided by weighting can be reproduced exactly
return poly.evaluate(x) / sqrt(1 - x * x);
}
};
// the integrators
Integrator integrator1 = new Trapezoidal(1e-8, 20); // using the trapezoidal rule
Integrator integrator2 = new Simpson(1e-8, 20); // using the Simpson rule
Integrator integrator3 = new GaussChebyshevQuadrature(2);
// the limits
double a = -1., b = 1.;
// the integrations
double I1 = integrator1.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the trapezoidal rule", a, b, I1));
double I2 = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Simpson rule", a, b, I2));
double I3 = integrator3.integrate(f, a, b);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %.16f, using the Gauss Hermite quadrature", a, b, I3));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[-1,1] f(x) dx = NaN, using the trapezoidal rule
S_[-1,1] f(x) dx = NaN, using the Simpson rule
S_[-1,1] f(x) dx = 4.7123889803846900, using the Gauss Hermite quadrature
```

Note that neither the trapezoidal nor the Simpson rule can compute this integral.

## 6.10 Integration by Substitution

The functional forms in Section [6.9](#500382_1_En_6_Chapter.xhtml#Sec25) are restrictive. For example, the interval to apply the Gauss-Legendre formula is [−1, 1]. Often, we want more flexibility in the interval. The other forms integrate from and/or until infinity, which makes it infeasible to apply simpler quadrature rules like trapezoidal or Simpson’s. Many integrands are difficult to calculate because they are complicated. There are also functions that cannot be evaluated at certain points due to singularity. Integration by substitution writes an integral in a simpler form so it is easier to compute for example by avoiding singularity. It can transform the interval to a desired range and to avoid infinity. Moreover, it speeds up computation by reducing the number of iterations needed for convergence. The substitution rule says that we find a change of variable, as shown here:

![$$ x=\varphi (t) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equep.png)

such that

![$$ dx={\varphi}^{\prime }(t) dt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equeq.png)

We can then replace the integral in *t* with an integral in *x*.

![$$ {\int}_a^bf\left(\varphi (t)\right){\varphi}^{\prime }(t) dx={\int}_{\varphi (a)}^{\varphi (b)}f(x) du $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equer.png)

An example will make it easier to understand. Suppose we want to calculate the following:

![$$ I={\int}_0^2t\cos \left({t}^2+1\right) dt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Eques.png)

We notice that if we set this:

![$$ x={t}^2+1 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equet.png)

then we have the following:

![$$ dx=2 tdt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equeu.png)

or the following:

![$$ \frac{1}{2} dx= tdt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equev.png)

Plugging these into the original integral and getting rid of *t*, we have the following:

![$$ I={\int}_0^2t\cos \left({t}^2+1\right) dx={\int}_{x=1}^{x=5}\frac{1}{2}\cos xdx $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equew.png)

The new integral in *x* is so much less intimidating.

![$$ I=\frac{1}{2}{\int}_1^5\cos xdx=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sin 5-\sin 1\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equex.png)

To do integration by substitution in NM Dev, we will need to specify the change of variable by inheriting the interface `SubstitutionRule`.

```
public interface SubstitutionRule {
/**
* the transformation: x(t)
*
* @return x(t)
*/
public UnivariateRealFunction x();
/**
* the first order derivative of the transformation: x'(t) = dx(t)/dt
*
* @return x'(t) = dx(t)/dt
*/
public UnivariateRealFunction dx();
/**
* the lower limit of the integral.
*
* @return the lower limit
*/
public double ta();
/**
* the upper limit of the integral.
*
* @return the upper limit
*/
public double tb();
}
```

The change of variable is specified in `x()`. We also need to specify the differential of the change of variable in `dx()`, as well as the limits `ta()` and `tb()`.

NM Dev has prebuilt a suite of substitution rules ready to be used out of the box.

### 6.10.1 Standard Interval

This transformation maps the integral interval from [*a*, *b*] to [−1, 1]. The substitution rule is as follows:

![$$ x(t)=\frac{\left(b-a\right)t+\left(a+b\right)}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equey.png)

![$$ {x}^{\prime }(t)=\frac{\left(b-a\right)}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equez.png)

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx={\int}_{-1}^1\frac{\left(b-a\right)}{2}f\left(\frac{\left(b-a\right)t+\left(a+b\right)}{2}\right) dt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfa.png)

Here’s an example:

```
double a = 0., b = 10.; // the limits
Integrator integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(3, NewtonCotes.Type.OPEN, 1e-8, 10);
Integrator integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(new StandardInterval(a, b), integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate(
new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double t) {
return t; // the original integrand
}
},
a, b // the original limits
);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,10] f(x) dx = 50.000000
```

### 6.10.2 Inverting Variable

This transformation is useful when the following happens:

1.  *b* →  ∞ , *a* > 0

2.  *a* →  −  ∞ , *b* < 0

3.  Any function that decreases toward infinity faster than ![$$ \frac{1}{x^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq26.png)

The integrator for this substitution should use an open formula to avoid computing for the endpoint where *t* = 0\. The substitution is as follows:

![$$ x(t)=\frac{1}{t} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfb.png)

![$$ {x}^{\prime }(t)=-\frac{1}{t^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfc.png)

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx={\int}_{1/b}^{1/a}\frac{1}{t^2}f(t) dt, ab&gt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfd.png)

Here’s an example:

```
double a = 1., b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(3, NewtonCotes.Type.OPEN, 1e-15, 10);
ChangeOfVariable integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(new InvertingVariable(a, b), integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate( // I = 1
new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return 1 / x / x; // the original integrand
}
},
a, b // the original limits
);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[1,Infinity] f(x) dx = 1.000000
```

### 6.10.3 Exponential

This transformation is good for when the lower limit is finite, the upper limit is infinite, and the integrand falls off exponentially. The integrator for this substitution should use an open formula to avoid computing for the endpoint where *t* = 0\. The substitution is as follows:

![$$ x(t)=-\log t $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfe.png)

![$$ {x}^{\prime }(t)=-\frac{1}{t} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equff.png)

![$$ {\int}_a^{\infty }f(x) dx={\int}_0^{e^a}\frac{f\left(-\log t\right)}{t} dt $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfg.png)

Here’s an example:

```
double a = 0., b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(3, NewtonCotes.Type.OPEN, 1e-15, 15);
ChangeOfVariable integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(new Exponential(a), integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate( // I = sqrt(PI)/2
new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return sqrt(x) * exp(-x); // the original integrand
}
},
a, b // the original limits
);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,Infinity] f(x) dx = 0.886227
```

### 6.10.4 Mixed Rule

The mixed rule is good for functions that fall off rapidly at infinity, e.g., *e*^(*x*) or ![$$ {e}^{x^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_IEq27.png). The integral interval is [0, ∞). The tricky part of using this transformation is to figure out a good range for *t*. If there is information about the integrand available, `SubstitutionRule.ta()` and `SubstitutionRule.tb()` should be overridden. The substitution is as follows:

![$$ x(t)={e}^{t-{e}^{-t}} $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfh.png)

Here’s an example:

```
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return exp(-x) * pow(x, -1.5) * sin(x / 2);
}
};
double a = 0., b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(2, NewtonCotes.Type.CLOSED, 1e-15, 7); // only 7 iteration!
ChangeOfVariable integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(new MixedRule(f, a, b, 1), integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b); // I = sqrt(PI * (sqrt(5) - 2))
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,Infinity] f(x) dx = 0.861179
```

### 6.10.5 Double Exponential

This transformation speeds up the convergence of the trapezoidal rule exponentially. It applies to a finite integral interval [*a*, *b*]. The tricky part of using this transformation is to figure out a good range for *t*. If there is information about the integrand available, `SubstitutionRule.ta()` and `SubstitutionRule.tb()` should be overridden. The substitution is as follows:

![$$ x(t)=\frac{b+a}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}\tanh \left(c\sinh t\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfi.png)

Here’s an example:

```
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return log(x) * log(1 - x);
}
};
double a = 0., b = 1.; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(2, NewtonCotes.Type.CLOSED, 1e-15, 6); // only 6 iterations!
ChangeOfVariable integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(new DoubleExponential(f, a, b, 1), integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b); // I = 2 - PI * PI / 6
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[0,1] f(x) dx = 0.355066
```

### 6.10.6 Double Exponential for Real Line

This transformation is good for the interval (−∞, ∞). The tricky part of using this transformation is to figure out a good range for *t*. If there is information about the integrand available, `SubstitutionRule.ta()` and `SubstitutionRule.tb()` should be overridden. The substitution is as follows:

![$$ x(t)=\sinh \left(c\sinh t\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfj.png)

Here’s an example:

```
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return exp(-x * x);
}
};
double a = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(3, NewtonCotes.Type.CLOSED, 1e-15, 6); // only 6 iterations!
ChangeOfVariable integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(new DoubleExponential4RealLine(f, a, b, 1), integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate(f, a, b); // sqrt(PI)
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[-Infinity,Infinity] f(x) dx = 1.772454
```

### 6.10.7 Double Exponential for Half Real Line

This transformation is good for the interval (0, ∞). The tricky part of using this transformation is to figure out a good range for *t*. If there is information about the integrand available, `SubstitutionRule.ta()` and `SubstitutionRule.tb()` should be overridden. The substitution is as follows:

![$$ x(t)=\exp \left(2c\sinh t\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfk.png)

Here’s an example:

```
UnivariateRealFunction f = new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return x / (exp(x) - 1);
}
};
double a = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY, b = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator
= new NewtonCotes(3, NewtonCotes.Type.OPEN, 1e-15, 15);
ChangeOfVariable instance
= new ChangeOfVariable(new DoubleExponential4HalfRealLine(f, a, b, 1), integrator);
double I = instance.integrate(f, a, b); // PI * PI / 6
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows:

```
S_[-Infinity,Infinity] f(x) dx = 1.772454
```

### 6.10.8 Power Law Singularity

This transformation is good for an integral that diverges at one of the end points.

For singularity at the lower limit, we have (*x* − *a*)^(−*γ*) diverging near *x* = *a*. 0 ≤ *γ* ≤ 1\. The substitution rule is as follows:

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx={\int}_0^{{\left(b-a\right)}^{1-\gamma }}\frac{t^{\frac{\gamma }{1-\gamma }}f\left({t}^{\frac{1}{1-\gamma }}+a\right)}{1-\gamma } dt,b&gt;a $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfl.png)

For singularity at the upper limit, we have (*x* − *b*)^(−*γ*) diverging near *x* = *b*. 0 ≤ *γ* ≤ 1\. The substitution rule is as follows:

![$$ {\int}_a^bf(x) dx={\int}_0^{{\left(b-a\right)}^{1-\gamma }}\frac{t^{\frac{\gamma }{1-\gamma }}f\left(b-{t}^{\frac{1}{1-\gamma }}\right)}{1-\gamma } dt,b&gt;a $$](images/500382_1_En_6_Chapter/500382_1_En_6_Chapter_TeX_Equfm.png)

A common case is when *γ* = 0.5.

Here’s an example:

```
double a = 1, b = 2; // the limits
NewtonCotes integrator1
= new NewtonCotes(3, NewtonCotes.Type.OPEN, 1e-15, 15);
ChangeOfVariable integrator2
= new ChangeOfVariable(
new PowerLawSingularity(
PowerLawSingularity.PowerLawSingularityType.LOWER,
0.5, // gamma = 0.5
a, b),
integrator1);
double I = integrator2.integrate( // I = 2
new AbstractUnivariateRealFunction() {
@Override
public double evaluate(double x) {
return 1 / sqrt(x - 1);
}
},
a, b
);
System.out.println(String.format("S_[%.0f,%.0f] f(x) dx = %f", a, b, I));
```

The output is as follows :

```
S_[1,2] f(x) dx = 2.000000
```

# 7. Ordinary Differential Equations

An ordinary differential equation (ODE) is an equation that involves the derivatives of one independent variable. The term “ordinary” is used in contrast with the term partial differential equation (PDE), which involves more than one independent variable. Differential equations arise in many contexts of mathematics and sciences. More often than not, it is easier to describe the changes, dynamics, or variations of a system than the system itself. The system itself can be complex, but its dynamics may be simple (or simpler). For instance, it is not always easy (or even feasible) to figure out the trajectory of an object to start with. By contrast, Newton’s famous second law of motion can describe the trajectory of any object from a football to a planet in a simple expression using an ODE.

![$$ F\left(x(t)\right)=m{a}^2=m\frac{d^2x(t)}{d{t}^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equa.png)

Moreover, many phenomena fundamentally relate different differential quantities together, e.g., rate of change or gradient, or curvature. For example, the previous ODE connects these quantities: position (or displacement) over time *x*(*t*), force *F*, time *t*, and mass *m*. The first derivative of a position function with respect to time is velocity; the second derivative is acceleration, *a*. Ordinary differential equations are ubiquitous in almost all sciences, such as physics and astronomy (celestial mechanics), meteorology (weather modeling), chemistry (reaction rates), biology (infectious diseases, genetic variation), ecology and population modeling (population competition), and economics (stock trends, interest rates, and market equilibrium price changes).

The numerical solution of ordinary differential equations is a branch of computational mathematics to solve ordinary differential equation problems. That is, we find a function that satisfies the ODE. The numerical solution is important because many ODEs cannot be solved analytically. Even if they can be, the solutions cannot be expressed in terms of elementary functions. In these cases, we can resort only to numerically solving them. The numerical solution is an approximation of the true solution of an ODE at certain discrete points. We need to study the existence, uniqueness, and stability of such a numerical solution.

## 7.1 Single-Step Method

Initial value problems are one class of ODE problem. An initial value problem (IVP) is an ordinary differential equation together with an initial condition that specifies the value of the unknown function at a given point in the domain. Modeling a system in physics or other sciences frequently amounts to solving an IVP. In that context, the differential equation is an equation that specifies how the system evolves with time given the initial conditions of the system at time zero. Mathematically, an initial value problem is a differential equation, as shown here:

![$$ {y}^{\prime }(t)=f\left(t,y(t)\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equb.png)

together with the initial condition, as shown here:

![$$ {y}_0=y\left({t}_0\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equc.png)

The solution to the IVP is a function *y* that is a solution to the differential equation and satisfies the initial condition. The concept can be extended to higher orders by treating the derivatives in the same way as an independent function. For a second-order ODE, we have this:

![$$ {y}^{\prime \prime }(t)=f\left(t,y(t),{y}^{\prime }(t)\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equd.png)

In general, it is assumed that the function *f* (*x*, *y*) satisfies the Lipschitz condition, as shown here:

![$$ \left|f\left(x,y\right)-f\Big(x,\bar{y}\Big)\right|\le L\left|y-\bar{y}\right| $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Eque.png)

*L* is a constant. The condition is basically saying that the function *f* cannot change too fast. This condition guarantees that the ODE has one and only one solution.

For example, we can find the solution of the following ODE:

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{y}^{\prime }=1-2 xy\\ {}y(0)=0\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equf.png)

A numerical solution gives the approximation values, *y*[1], *y*[2], …, *y*[*n*], *y*[*n* + 1], of *y*(*x*) at a set of discrete points, as shown here:

![$$ {x}_0&lt;{x}_1&lt;{x}_2&lt;\cdots &lt;{x}_n&lt;{x}_{n+1}&lt;\cdots $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equg.png)

*h*[*i*] = *x*[*i* + 1] − *x*[*i*] is called the *step size*. Unless it’s otherwise specified, we assume that the step size is equal and equally spaced.

Conceptually, we can solve an ODE in the following manner. We already know the value *y*(*x*[0]) = *y*[0] from the initial condition. To find *y*(*x*[1]) = *y*(*x*[0] + *h*), we can use an approximation: ∆*y*(*x*) ≈ *y*^′(*x*)*h*. So, we have this:

![$$ y\left({x}_1\right)=y\left({x}_0+h\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equh.png)

![$$ =y\left({x}_0\right)+\Delta y\left({x}_0\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equi.png)

![$$ =y\left({x}_0\right)+{y}^{\prime}\left({x}_0\right)h $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equj.png)

We can repeat this to iterate for *y*(*x*[2]) = *y*(*x*[1]) + *y*^′(*x*[1])*h* and *y*(*x*[3]) = *y*(*x*[2]) + *y*^′(*x*[2])*h*, and so on and so forth, step-by-step. This is the general idea of how to solve an ODE numerically. This family of methods is called the step-by-step method. Figure [7-1](#500382_1_En_7_Chapter.xhtml#Fig1) shows a numerical solution to the problem.

![../images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Fig1_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Fig1_HTML.jpg)

Figure 7-1

A numerical solution to the IVP using the step-by-step method

### 7.1.1 Euler’s Method (Polygon Method)

Euler’s method is a first-order numerical procedure for solving ordinary differential equations with a given initial value. It is the most basic explicit method for the numerical integration of ordinary differential equations and is the simplest Runge-Kutta method (discussed in Section 7.1.2). Being a first-order method, its local error (error per step) is proportional to the square of the step size, and the global error (error at a given time or value) is proportional to the step size. The accuracy is not high. It also suffers from a stability problem. For these reasons, Euler’s method is not often used in practice. It, however, illustrates some basic ideas in numerical integration. Euler’s method serves as the basis to construct more complicated methods.

#### 7.1.1.1 Euler’s Formula

We can use Taylor expansion to derive Euler’s formula .

![$$ y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)=y\left({x}_n+h\right)=y\left({x}_n\right)+{y}^{\prime}\left({x}_n\right)h+\frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq1.png), *ξ*[*n*] ∈ (*x*[*n*], *x*[*n* + 1])

![$$ y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)=y\left({x}_n\right)+ hf\left[{x}_n,y\left({x}_n\right)\right]+\frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq2.png), *n* = 0, 1, 2, ⋯

When *h* is sufficiently small, we can ignore the higher-order term ![$$ \frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq3.png) and get an approximation, as shown here:

![$$ y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)\approx y\left({x}_n\right)+ hf\left[{x}_n,y\left({x}_n\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equk.png)

Using the notation that *y*[*n* + 1] ≈ *y*(*x*[*n* + 1]), Euler’s formula is as follows:

*y*[*n* + 1] = *y*[*n*] + *hf* (*x*[*n*], *y*[*n*]), *n* = 0, 1, 2, ⋯

The local truncation error for this formula is the error in the *n*-th step, which is given by ![$$ \frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq4.png), which is proportional to the square of the step size *h*². The global error, on the other hand, is the error accumulated from the beginning to the current step. See Figure [7-2](#500382_1_En_7_Chapter.xhtml#Fig2).

![../images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Fig2_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Fig2_HTML.jpg)

Figure 7-2

Euler’s method and the approximation errors

Euler’s method is a polyline method rather than a tangent method. Except that the first point is a tangent on the curve, the function is approximated by a piecewise polyline.

#### 7.1.1.2 Implicit Euler Formula

We can derive an implicit formula or a backward formula for Euler’s method. The difference quotient is as follows:

![$$ {y}^{\prime}\left({x}_{n+1}\right)\approx \frac{y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)-y\left({x}_n\right)}{x_{n+1}-{x}_n}=\frac{y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)-y\left({x}_n\right)}{h_n} $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equl.png)

Assuming that *y*[*n*] = *y*(*x*[*n*]) and we already know that *y*^′(*x*[*n* + 1]) = *f* (*x*[*n* + 1], *y*(*x*[*n* + 1])), the implicit (backward) Euler formula is as follows:

*y*[*n* + 1] = *y*[*n*] + *hf* (*x*[*n* + 1], *y*[*n* + 1]), *n* = 0, 1, 2, ⋯

This formula is called an implicit formula because it has *y*[*n* + 1] on both the left- and right-hand sides. Unlike an explicit formula where you just need to plug in the numbers to compute *y*[*n* + 1], computing using an implicit formula involves solving equations for *y*[*n* + 1].

One way to solve the equation is to use an iterative method. We start with an initial guess of what *y*[*n* + 1] may be, ![$$ {y}_{n+1}^{(0)} $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq5.png). Then we plug it into the right-hand side to compute the next guesstimate ![$$ {y}_{n+1}^{(1)} $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq6.png). We repeat until it converges. Specifically, the iteration formula is as follows:

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{y}_{n+1}^{(0)}={y}_n+ hf\left({x}_n,{y}_n\right)\\ {}{y}_{n+1}^{\left(k+1\right)}={y}_n+ hf\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}^{(k)}\right)\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq7.png), *k* = 0, 1, ⋯

![$$ \left|{y}_{n+1}^{\left(k+1\right)}-{y}_{n+1}^{(k)}\right|&lt;\varepsilon $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equ1.png)

We study the local truncation error of the implicit formula. Given this:

![$$ {y}_{n+1}={y}_n+ hf\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}\right)={y}_n+h{y}^{\prime}\left({x}_{n+1}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equm.png)

![$$ {y}^{\prime}\left({x}_{n+1}\right)={y}^{\prime}\left({x}_n+h\right)={y}^{\prime}\left({x}_n\right)+{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right)h $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equn.png)

and substituting the second equation into the first one, we have the following:

![$$ {y}_{n+1}={y}_n+h{y}^{\prime}\left({x}_n\right)+{h}^2{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equo.png)

We also have this:

![$$ y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)=y\left({x}_n\right)+ hf\left({x}_n,y\left({x}_n\right)\right)+\frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equp.png)

Assuming that *y*[*n*] = *y*(*x*[*n*]) and subtracting the first equation from the second one, we have the local truncation error, as shown here:

![$$ y\left({x}_{n+1}\right)-{y}_{n+1}=-\frac{h^2}{2}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({\xi}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equq.png)

Alternatively , the local truncation error of the implicit Euler formula is approximately the following:

![$$ -\frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({x}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equr.png)

#### 7.1.1.3 Trapezoidal Formula

Note that the local truncation errors of the explicit and implicit methods differ by only a negative sign. That is,

![$$ {y}_{n+1}={y}_n+ hf\left({x}_n,{y}_n\right)+\frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({x}_n\right)+o\left({h}^3\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equs.png)

![$$ {y}_{n+1}={y}_n+ hf\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}\right)-\frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({x}_n\right)+o\left({h}^3\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equt.png)

Adding these two equations together and dividing by 2, we eliminate ![$$ \frac{h^2}{2!}{y}^{{\prime\prime}}\left({x}_n\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq8.png) and get this:

![$$ {y}_{n+1}={y}_n+\frac{h}{2}\left[f\left({x}_n,{y}_n\right)+f\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}\right)\right]+o\left({h}^3\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equu.png)

The trapezoidal formula is as follows (by ignoring *o*(*h*³)):

![$$ {y}_{n+1}={y}_n+\frac{h}{2}\left[f\left({x}_n,{y}_n\right)+f\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equv.png)

The trapezoidal formula is also an implicit formula. It can be solved by using an iterative method as follows:

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{y}_{n+1}^{(0)}={y}_n+ hf\left({x}_n,{y}_n\right)\\ {}{y}_{n+1}^{\left(k+1\right)}={y}_n+\frac{h}{2}\left[f\left({x}_n,{y}_n\right)+f\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}^{(k)}\right)\right]\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq9.png), *k* = 0, 1, ⋯

This iteration method will converge because

![$$ \left|{y}_{n+1}-{y}_{n+1}^{\left(k+1\right)}\right|=\frac{h}{2}\left|f\left({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}\right)-f\Big({x}_{n+1},{y}_{n+1}^{(k)}\Big)\right| $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equw.png)

It has been assumed that *f* (*x*, *y*) satisfies the Lipschitz condition.

![$$ \left|f\left(x,y\right)-f\Big(x,\bar{y}\Big)\right|\le L\left|y-\bar{y}\right| $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equx.png)

That is,

![$$ \left|{y}_{n+1}-{y}_{n+1}^{\left(k+1\right)}\right|\le \frac{Lh}{2}\left|{y}_{n+1}-{y}_{n+1}^{(k)}\right| $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equy.png)

Take ![$$ \frac{Lh}{2}&lt;1 $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_IEq10.png) and then the following:

![$$ \left|{y}_{n+1}-{y}_{n+1}^{\left(k+1\right)}\right|\le \left|{y}_{n+1}-{y}_{n+1}^{(k)}\right| $$](images/500382_1_En_7_Chapter/500382_1_En_7_Chapter_TeX_Equz.png)

Hence , we have (conditional) convergence. The trapezoidal formula is more accurate than either the explicit and implicit formula (first-order accuracy *o*(*h*²)), and it has the second-order accuracy *o*(*h*³).

#### 7.1.1.4 Prediction-Correction Method

While the trapezoid formula gives good accuracy *o*(*h*³), the workload is too large. The prediction-correction method improves upon Euler’s formula by using the trapezoidal formula but doing only one round of iteration. Specifically, we have this:
