### 10.2.4 The Algebra of Simplex Method

In the previous section we discussed the geometry of the simplex method. We can also cast the algorithm in the general optimization framework in Section 10.1.1\. Given a vertex ***x***[***k***] (nondegenerate meaning that it has exactly *n* edges or active constraints), a vertex ***x***[***k +*** **1**] is said to be adjacent to ***x***[***k***] if ***A***[***ak +*** **1**] differs from ***A***[***ak***] by exactly one row.

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_{\boldsymbol{a}\boldsymbol{k}}=\left[\begin{array}{c}{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}\mathbf{1}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\\ {}{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}\mathbf{2}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\\ {}\boldsymbol{\vdots}\\ {}{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}\boldsymbol{n}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equeb.png)

where ![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq31.png) are the coefficients of the *ji*-th constraint. Associated with ***A***[***ak***] is the set of indices of active constraints.

![$$ {\mathfrak{I}}_k=\left\{j1,j2,\dots jn\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equec.png)

where *ji* stands for an index in the original variable.

In other words, if ![$$ {\mathfrak{I}}_k $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq32.png) and ![$$ {\mathfrak{I}}_{k+1} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq33.png) have exactly (*n* − 1) same members, ***x***[***k***] and ***x***[***k +*** **1**] are adjacent. As vertex ***x***[***k***], the simplex algorithm checks if ***x***[***k***] is a minimizer. If it is not, it finds an adjacent ***x***[***k +*** **1**] that gives a smaller objective function value. If a minimizer exists and there are a finite number of vertices, the simplex algorithm will always find a solution in a finite number of iterations.

The KKT conditions say that there exists a ***λ***[***k***] ∈ *ℝ*^(*n*) such that

![$$ \boldsymbol{c}={\boldsymbol{A}}_{\boldsymbol{ak}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equed.png)

and that ***x***[***k***] is a minimizer if this is true:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\boldsymbol{\ge}\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equee.png)

In other words, ***x***[***k***] is not a minimizer if and only if at least one component of ***λ***[***k***], say the *l*-th component (***λ***[***k***])[*l*], is negative. That is,

![$$ {\left({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\right)}_l&lt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equef.png)

In our general optimization algorithm, the next (and adjacent) vertex is given by the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}+\mathbf{1}}={\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\alpha}_k{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equeg.png)

It can be shown that a feasible descent direction ***d***[***k***] is characterized by the following:

***A***[***ak***]***d***[***k***] ***≥*** **0**, ***c***^(***T***)***d***[***k***] ***<*** 0

To find the edge ***d***[***k***], we solve for the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_{\boldsymbol{ak}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}={\boldsymbol{e}}_{\boldsymbol{l}}\boldsymbol{\ge}\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equeh.png)

where ***e***[***l***] is *l*-th coordinate vector (i.e., the *l*-th column of the *n* × *n* identity matrix).

Then, we have the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{c}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}={\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{A}}_{\boldsymbol{ak}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}={\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{e}}_{\boldsymbol{l}}={\left({\boldsymbol{\lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\right)}_l&lt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equei.png)

Therefore, ***d***[***k***] is a feasible descent direction.

Moreover, for *i* ≠ *l*, we have this:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\left({\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\alpha}_k{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\right)={\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\alpha}_k{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}={b}_{ji} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equej.png)

We can solve *α*[*i*] for each *i* in the index set ![$$ {\mathcal{I}}_k $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq34.png) of the inactive constraints at ***x***[***k***] and with ![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&lt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq35.png)

![$$ {\mathcal{I}}_k=\left\{i:{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}-{b}_{ji}&gt;0,{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{ji}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&lt;0\ \right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equek.png)

![$$ {\alpha}_k=\underset{i\in {\mathcal{I}}_k}{\min}\left\{{\alpha}_i\right\}=\underset{i\in {\mathcal{I}}_k}{\min}\left(\frac{b_i-{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equel.png)

The NM Dev class `LPRevisedSimplexSolver` implements this algebraic form of simplex algorithm as described in Antoniou & Lu (2007). We can use this solver to solve the same LP problem in Chen, Batson, & Dang (2009) that we solved in the previous section.

We need to change this one line from this:

```
LPTwoPhaseSolver solver = new LPTwoPhaseSolver();
```

to this:

```
LPRevisedSimplexSolver solver = new LPRevisedSimplexSolver(1e-8);
```

to use a different solver.

![$$ \underset{x_1,{x}_2}{\min }-5{x}_1+2{x}_2 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equem.png)

subject to,

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{x}_1+3{x}_2\ge 9\\ {}-{x}_1+2{x}_2\le 5\\ {}3{x}_1+2{x}_2\ge 19\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equen.png)

```
// construct an LP problem
LPProblemImpl1 problem = new LPProblemImpl1(
new DenseVector(-5.0, 2.0), // c
new LinearGreaterThanConstraints(
new DenseMatrix( // A1
new double[][]{
{1.0, 3.0}}),
new DenseVector(9.0)), // b1
new LinearLessThanConstraints(
new DenseMatrix( // A2
new double[][]{
{-1.0, 2.0},
{3.0, 2.0}}),
new DenseVector(5.0, 19.0)), // b2
null,
null);
// solve the LP problem using the algebraic LP solver
LPRevisedSimplexSolver solver = new LPRevisedSimplexSolver(1e-8);
LPMinimizer solution = solver.solve(problem).minimizer();
System.out.printf("minimum = %f%n", solution.minimum());
System.out.printf("minimizer = %s%n", solution.minimizer());
```

The output is as follows:

```
minimum = -25.571429
minimizer = [5.571429, 1.142857]
```

They are exactly the same result as from the other two-phase solver.

## 10.3 Quadratic Programming

Quadratic programming (QP) is to minimize a quadratic objective function subject to linear constraints. It has important applications such as in quantitative finance. Also, it is often used to solve subproblems in other more general, nonlinear constrained optimization, such as sequential quadratic programming. The problem is often stated as follows:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x}}{\min }f\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hx}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{p} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equeo.png)

subject to,

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}x\ge \boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equep.png)

where ***A*** ∈ *ℝ*^(*p* × *n*) for *p* linear constraints for *n* variables. We usually assume that the matrix ***A*** is symmetric, of full rank, and positive semidefinite ***A*** ≽ 0.

If the Hessian matrix ***H*** ≽ 0 is positive semidefinite, then the problem is a convex optimization problem. The problem can be solved in (weakly) polynomial time. Otherwise, the problem is NP-hard. There can be several stationary points and local minima for a nonconvex problem. In fact, even if ***H*** has only one negative eigenvalue, the problem is strongly NP-hard.

An important application of QP is modern portfolio theory. Suppose we want to allocate a pool of money to buy *n* stocks and hold the portfolio for one year. Although the exact return for a stock one year later is unknown, we can model the annual return, *r*[*i*], for stock *i* as a random variable, say normal distribution. That is,

![$$ {r}_i\sim N\left({\mu}_i,{\sigma}_i\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equeq.png)

Because stocks are not exactly independent, they tend to move up and down in tandem. They are correlated. The correlation between stock *i* and stock *j* is as follows:

![$$ {\rho}_{ij}=\frac{\mathrm{E}\left[\left({r}_i-{\mu}_i\right)\left({r}_j-{\mu}_j\right)\right]}{\sigma_i{\sigma}_j} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equer.png)

The investor’s decision is to decide what portion or weight, *w*[*i*], of the pool of money to put into each stock to construct their portfolio. The expected return of the portfolio is then as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}\left[R\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{w}_i{r}_i\right]=\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{w}_i\mathrm{E}\left[{r}_i\right]=\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{w}_i{\mu}_i={\boldsymbol{w}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\mu} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Eques.png)

The variance of the portfolio is as follows:

![$$ Var\left[R\right]=\mathrm{E}\left[{\left(R-\mathrm{E}\left[R\right]\right)}^2\right]=\sum \limits_{i=1}^n\sum \limits_{j=1}^n{w}_i{w}_j{\sigma}_i{\sigma}_j{\rho}_{ij}={\boldsymbol{w}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \boldsymbol{w} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equet.png)

where **Σ** is the *n* × *n* symmetric positive semidefinite covariance matrix defined as follows:

![$$ {\Sigma}_{ij}={\rho}_{ij}{\sigma}_i{\sigma}_j $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equeu.png)

Markowitz proposed that the investor should find a weighting so that the expected return of the portfolio is maximized while the risk (measured by portfolio variance) is minimized. This essentially sets up the following QP problem:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{w}}{\min}\lambda {\boldsymbol{w}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma} \boldsymbol{w}-{\boldsymbol{w}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\mu} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equev.png)

subject to,

![$$ \sum \limits_{i=1}^n{w}_i=1 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equew.png)

The sum of all weights is equal to 100 percent. We can impose other constraints such as a minimum weight for each stock at, for example, 0 percent. This is saying that no short selling is allowed. This inequality constraints can be written as follows:

![$$ \boldsymbol{w}\ge 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equex.png)

*λ* > 0 is called the risk-averse coefficient . An investor who is more conservative to minimize risk will choose a smaller *λ*. On the other hand, a more aggressive investor who aims for a bigger expected return and can sustain a possible bigger drawdown will choose a bigger *λ*. Changing *λ* gives different portfolios (different weightings) that satisfy the condition that no other portfolio exists with a higher expected return but with the same standard deviation of return (i.e., the risk) for that *λ*. The set of these optimal portfolios (for different *λ*s) together draw what we call the efficient frontier. See Figure [10-11](#500382_1_En_10_Chapter.xhtml#Fig11).

![../images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig11_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig11_HTML.jpg)

Figure 10-11

Efficient frontier of portfolios

### 10.3.1 Convex QP Problems with Only Equality Constraints

Let’s start with an easy convex QP problem that we can solve analytically. A convex QP problem with only equality constraints is stated as follows:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x}}{\min }f\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hx}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{p} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equey.png)

subject to,

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}x=\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equez.png)

where ***H*** ≽ 0, ***A*** ≽ 0, ***A*** ∈ *ℝ*^(*p* × *n*), ***A*** symmetric and of full rank with *p* < *n*.

It can be shown that the solution ***x*** takes this form:

![$$ \boldsymbol{x}={\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}\boldsymbol{\phi} +{\boldsymbol{A}}^{+}\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfa.png)

where ***V***[***r***] is composed of the last *n* − *p* columns of ***V***. ***V*** is from singular-value decomposition of ***A = U*****Σ*****V***^(***T***). ***A***^(***+***) is the Moore-Penrose inverse of ***A***.

Using this solution form, the problem can be reformulated as an equivalent unconstrained minimization problem, as shown here:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{\phi}}{\min}\hat{f}\left(\boldsymbol{\phi} \right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}\boldsymbol{\phi} +{\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\hat{\boldsymbol{p}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfb.png)

where

![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}={\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{H}{\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfc.png)

![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}={\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\left(\boldsymbol{H}{\boldsymbol{A}}^{+}\boldsymbol{b}+\boldsymbol{p}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfd.png)

If ***H*** ≻ 0 is positive definite, then so is ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}\succ 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq36.png) The unique global minimizer of the problem is as follows:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}={\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{\ast}+{\boldsymbol{A}}^{+}\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfe.png)

where ***ϕ***^(***∗***) is the solution of the linear system:

![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}\boldsymbol{\phi} =-\hat{\boldsymbol{p}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equff.png)

If ***H*** ≽ 0 is positive semidefinite, then ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq37.png) is either positive definite or positive semidefinite. If ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}\succ 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq38.png) is positive definite, then ***x***^(***∗***) is the unique global minimizer of the problem. If ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}\succcurlyeq 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq39.png)≽ 0 is positive semidefinite, then there are two possibilities. If ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq40.png) can be expressed as a linear combination of columns of ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq41.png), then *f*(*x*) has infinitely many global minimizers. Otherwise, there is no minimizer.

Let’s illustrate this method using the following QP problem in Antoniou & Lu (2007):

![$$ \underset{x_1,{x}_2,{x}_3}{\min }f\left({x}_1,{x}_2,{x}_3\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left({x}_1^2+{x}_2^2\right)+2{x}_1+{x}_2-{x}_3 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfg.png)

subject to,

![$$ \boldsymbol{Ax}=\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfh.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}=\left[0\kern0.5em 1\kern0.5em 1\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq42.png), ***b*** = 1

The objective function in matrix form is as follows:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x}}{\min }f\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hx}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{p} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfi.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{H}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&amp; 0&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 1&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 0&amp; 0\end{array}\right]\succcurlyeq 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfj.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{p}=\left[\begin{array}{c}2\\ {}1\\ {}-1\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfk.png)

The singular-value decomposition of ***A*** gives the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}=\left[\kern0.5em \begin{array}{cc}1&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\ {}0&amp; -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfl.png)

![$$ {\mathbf{A}}^{+}=\left[\begin{array}{c}0\\ {}0.5\\ {}0.5\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfm.png)

Therefore, we have the following:

![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{H}}={\boldsymbol{V}}_r^T\boldsymbol{H}{\boldsymbol{V}}_r=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{array}\right]\succ 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfn.png)

The unique global minimizer is as follows:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}={\boldsymbol{V}}_{\boldsymbol{r}}{\boldsymbol{\phi}}^{\ast}+{\boldsymbol{A}}^{+}\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfo.png)

![$$ =\left[\kern0.75em \begin{array}{cc}1&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\\ {}0&amp; -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{array}\ \right]\times \left[\ \begin{array}{c}-2\\ {}-3.5355\end{array}\ \right]+\left[\ \begin{array}{c}0\\ {}0.5\\ {}0.5\end{array}\ \right]\left[1\right]=\left[\ \begin{array}{c}-2\\ {}-2\\ {}3\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfp.png)

In NM Dev, the class `QuadraticFunction` constructs a quadratic function of this form:

![$$ f\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hx}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{c} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfq.png)

The class signature is as follows:

```
public class QuadraticFunction extends AbstractRealScalarFunction {
/**
* Construct a quadratic function of this form: \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \times
* x'Hx + x'p + c\).
*
* @param H a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix
* @param p a vector
* @param c a constant
*/
public QuadraticFunction(Matrix H, Vector p, double c);
/**
* Construct a quadratic function of this form: \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \times
* x'Hx + x'p\).
*
* @param H a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix
* @param p a vector
*/
public QuadraticFunction(Matrix H, Vector p);
/**
* Copy constructor.
*
* @param f a quadratic function
*/
public QuadraticFunction(QuadraticFunction f);
public ImmutableMatrix Hessian();
public ImmutableVector p();
@Override
public Double evaluate(Vector z);
@Override
public String toString();
}
```

The class `QPSimpleMinimizer` is a utility class that has a collection of utility functions to solve unconstrained QP problems and QP problems with only equality constraints. Both these problems can be solved analytically. The following code reproduces the previous example:

```
//construct the QP problem with only equality constraints
DenseMatrix H = new DenseMatrix(
new double[][]{
{1, 0, 0},
{0, 1, 0},
{0, 0, 0}
});
DenseVector p = new DenseVector(2, 1, -1);
QuadraticFunction f = new QuadraticFunction(H, p);
System.out.println("minimizing:");
System.out.println(f);
// equality constraints
DenseMatrix A = new DenseMatrix(
new double[][]{
{0, 1, 1}
});
DenseVector b = new DenseVector(1.);
LinearEqualityConstraints Aeq = new LinearEqualityConstraints(A, b);
// solve a QP problem with only equality constraints
QPSolution soln = QPSimpleMinimizer.solve(f, Aeq);
Vector x = soln.minimizer();
double fx = f.evaluate(x);
System.out.printf("f(%s) = %f%n", x, fx);
System.out.printf("is unique = %b%n", soln.isUnique());
```

The output is as follows:

```
minimizing:
1/2 * x'3x3
[,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,] 1.000000, 0.000000, 0.000000,
[2,] 0.000000, 1.000000, 0.000000,
[3,] 0.000000, 0.000000, 0.000000, x + x'[2.000000, 1.000000, -1.000000]
f([-2.000000, -2.000000, 3.000000] ) = -5.000000
is unique = true
```

NM Dev computes the same optimal solution ![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}=\left[\begin{array}{c}-2\\ {}-2\\ {}3\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq43.png) and the minimum value −5.

### 10.3.2 Active-Set Methods for Strictly Convex QP Problems

In general, a QP problem can be stated as follows:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x}}{\min }f\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hx}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{p} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfr.png)

subject to,

![$$ \boldsymbol{Ax}\boldsymbol{\ge}\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfs.png)

where ***A*** ∈ *R*^(*p* × *n*).

Without loss of generality, we skip the equality constraints because they can be eliminated as in Section 10.3.1.

The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions at a minimizer ***x*** are given by the following:

![$$ \boldsymbol{Hx}+\boldsymbol{p}-{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\mu} =\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equft.png)

![$$ \left({\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{x}-{b}_i\right){\mu}_i=0,i=1,2,\dots, p $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfu.png)

![$$ {\mu}_i\ge 0,i=1,2,\dots, p $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfv.png)

Suppose solution ***x***^(***∗***) is in the interior of the feasible region. (Unlike LP where a solution must be on the boundary, the solution for a QP problem can be inside the feasible region.) Then we have this:

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}-\boldsymbol{b}&gt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfw.png)

This implies the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\ast}=\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfx.png)

Then we have this:

![$$ \boldsymbol{H}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}+\boldsymbol{p}=\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfy.png)

The unique global minimizer ***x***^(***∗***) is the solution to this linear system, as shown here:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}=-{\boldsymbol{H}}^{-\mathbf{1}}\boldsymbol{p} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equfz.png)

#### 10.3.2.1 Primal Active-Set Method

If the solution ***x***^(***∗***) is not an interior point but on the boundary of feasible region, the next search direction is to consider the active constraints at the current iterate point ***x*** as a set of equality constraints while ignoring the other constraints. This is the active-set method to solve a general convex QP problem.

Let ***x***[***k***] be a feasible iterate point in the *k*-th iterations. Let *J*[*k*] be the index set of active constraints, namely, those constraints with ![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{x}-{b}_i=\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq44.png) which is called an active set. The next iteration, as in the general optimization algorithm in Section 10.1.1, is as follows:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}+\mathbf{1}}={\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\boldsymbol{d}={\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\alpha}_k{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equga.png)

Constraints that are active at ***x***[***k***] remain active at ***x***[***k +*** **1**] if the following is true:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}+\mathbf{1}}-{b}_j=0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq45.png), *j* ∈ *J*[*k*]

Multiplying ![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}}^{\boldsymbol{T}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq46.png) on both sides of the next iterate equation, we have this:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq47.png), *j* ∈ *J*[*k*]

The objective function at ***x***[***k***] + ***d*** is as follows:

![$$ {f}_k\left(\boldsymbol{d}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{d}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hd}+{\boldsymbol{d}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}+{c}_k $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgb.png)

where

![$$ {\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\boldsymbol{p}+{\boldsymbol{Hx}}_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgc.png)

and *c*[*k*] is a constant.

A major step in the active set method is to solve this following QP subproblem with only equality constraints, as shown here:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{d}}{\min}\hat{f}\left(\boldsymbol{d}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{d}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hd}+{\boldsymbol{d}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgd.png)

subject to,

![$$ {\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{j}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq48.png), *j* ∈ *J*[*k*]

This can be solved using the method in Section 10.3.1\. The primal active-set algorithm is as follows:

**Primal Active-Set Algorithm**

**Step 1**

Start with a feasible initial point ***x***[**0**].

Identify the initial active set *J*[0].

Form matrix ***A***[***a*****0**] as a submatrix of ***A*** using only the active constraints in *J*[0].

Set *k* = 0.

**Step 2**

Compute ***g***[***k***] = ***p*** + ***Hx***[***k***].

Use ***g***[***k***] to check whether ***d***[***k***] will be zero. If ***d***[***k***] is not zero, go to **step 4**.

**Step 3**

(***d***[***k***] ***=*** **0**)

Solve for ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq49.png) using ![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_{\boldsymbol{ak}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}={\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq50.png).

If ![$$ \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}\boldsymbol{\ge}\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq51.png), output ***x***[***k***] as the solution and terminate.

Otherwise, remove the index that is associated with the most negative Lagrange multiplier from ***J***[***k***].

**Step 4**

(***d***[***k***] ***≠*** **0**)

Solve for ***d***[***k***] using the sub-QP problem with only equality constraints.

**Step 5**

Compute *a*[*k*].

![$$ {\alpha}_k=\min \left\{1,\kern0.5em \underset{i\notin {J}_k,{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}&lt;0}{\min}\frac{b_i-{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{{\boldsymbol{a}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{d}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equge.png)

Set ***x***[***k +*** **1**] = ***x***[***k***] + *α*[*k*]***d***[***k***].

**Step 6**

If *α*[*k*] < 1, build *J*[*k* + 1] by adding the index that yields the minimum to *J*[*k*] in **step 5**.

Otherwise, let *J*[*k*] = *J*[*k* + 1].

**Step 7**

Set *k* = *k* + 1.

Repeat from **step 2**.

Consider this example problem in Nocedal & Wright (2006):

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x}}{\min }q\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)={\left({x}_1-1\right)}^2+{\left({x}_2-2.5\right)}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgf.png)

The constraints are as follows:

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{x}_1-2{x}_2+2\ge 0\\ {}-{x}_1-2{x}_2+6\ge 0\\ {}-{x}_1+2{x}_2+2\ge 0\\ {}{x}_1\ge 0\\ {}{x}_2\ge 0\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgg.png)

We can write the problem in matrix form.

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x}}{\min }f\left(\boldsymbol{x}\right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{Hx}+{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{p} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgh.png)

subject to,

![$$ \boldsymbol{Ax}\boldsymbol{\ge}\boldsymbol{b} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgi.png)

where

![$$ \boldsymbol{H}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 2\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgj.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{p}=\left[\begin{array}{c}-2\\ {}-5\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgk.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{cc}1&amp; -2\\ {}-1&amp; -2\\ {}-1&amp; 2\\ {}1&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 1\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgl.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{b}=\left[\begin{array}{c}-2\\ {}-6\\ {}-2\\ {}0\\ {}0\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgm.png)

(Note that these two formulations have different constant terms, but they are irrelevant to the solution.)

Pictorially, we have Figure [10-12](#500382_1_En_10_Chapter.xhtml#Fig12).

![../images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig12_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig12_HTML.jpg)

Figure 10-12

A quadratic programming problem

Figure [10-12](#500382_1_En_10_Chapter.xhtml#Fig12) shows the feasible region, the boundary, the contour of the objective function, and the constraint labels ***a***[***i***].

Suppose our initial iterate point is ***x***^(**0**) = [2, 0]^(*T*) (here a superscript indicates the number of iterations, and a subscript indicates the component). There are two active constraints for this vertex, ***a***[**3**] and ***a***[**5**]. ***a***[**3**]***x***^(**0**) ***= a***[**5**]***x***^(**0**) ***=*** **0**. The working set is *J*[0] = {3, 5}. The solution to the QP subproblem is ***d***^(**0**) ***=*** **0**. We need to solve for the Lagrange multipliers in the KKT conditions to check if it is a minimum point.

![$$ \left[\begin{array}{cc}-1&amp; 2\\ {}0&amp; 1\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{c}{\hat{\mu}}_1\\ {}{\hat{\mu}}_2\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}2\\ {}-5\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgn.png)

That is, we have this:

![$$ \left[\begin{array}{c}{\hat{\mu}}_3\\ {}{\hat{\mu}}_5\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}-2\\ {}-1\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgo.png)

This does not meet the non-negativity requirement, meaning that the minimum has not been found. We remove constraint 3, ***a***[**3**], from the working set because it has the biggest absolute value of the Lagrange multipliers.

In the next iteration *k* = 1, the active working set is now *J*[1] = {5}. ***x***^(**1**) = ***x***^(**0**) = [2, 0]^(*T*) because the last iteration does not move the search point. ***d***^(**1**) ***=*** [−1, 0]^(*T*). The step-length formula yields *α*[1] = 1\. The new iterate is ***x***^(**2**) = [1, 0]^(*T*).

In the next iteration *k* = 2, ***x***^(**2**) = [1, 0]^(*T*). ***d***^(**2**) ***=*** **0**. ![$$ {\hat{\mu}}_5=-5 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq52.png). We drop ***a***[**5**] from the working set. It is now empty, *J*[1] = { }.

In the next iteration *k* = 3, ***x***^(**3**) = [1, 0]^(*T*) because ***d***^(**2**) ***=*** **0**. Because the working set is empty, the QP subproblem is unconstrained. Solving it gives ***d***^(**3**) ***=*** [0, 2.5]^(*T*). The step-length formula yields *α*[3] = 0.6\. The new iterate is ***x***^(**4**) = [1, 1.5]^(*T*).

In the next iteration *k* = 4, ***x***^(**4**) = [1, 1.5]^(*T*). There is a single blocking constraint ***a***[**1**]. The first constraint is added to the working set, *J*[4] = {1}. ***d***^(**4**) ***=*** [0.4, 0.2]^(*T*). *α*[4] = 1\. The new iterate is ***x***^(**5**) = [1.4, 1.7]^(*T*). The working set remains unchanged.

In the next iteration *k* = 5, ***x***^(**5**) = [1.4, 1.7]^(*T*). ***d***^(**5**) ***=*** **0**. Checking the KKT conditions gives ![$$ {\hat{\mu}}_1=0.8&gt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq53.png). The minimizer has been found. We have the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}=\left[\begin{array}{c}1.4\\ {}1.7\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgp.png)

The following NM Dev code solves this QP problem:

```
// construct a quadratic function
Matrix H = new DenseMatrix(new double[][]{
{2, 0},
{0, 2}
});
Vector p = new DenseVector(new double[]{-2, -5});
QuadraticFunction f = new QuadraticFunction(H, p);
// construct the linear inequality constraints
Matrix A = new DenseMatrix(new double[][]{
{1, -2},
{-1, -2},
{-1, 2},
{1, 0},
{0, 1}
});
Vector b = new DenseVector(new double[]{-2, -6, -2, 0, 0});
LinearGreaterThanConstraints greater
= new LinearGreaterThanConstraints(A, b);// x >= 0
// construct the QP problem
QPProblem problem = new QPProblem(f, null, greater);
// construct a primal active set solver
double epsion = Math.sqrt(PrecisionUtils.autoEpsilon(problem.f().Hessian()));
QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer solver1
= new QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer(
epsion, // precision
Integer.MAX_VALUE // max number of iterations
);
// solve the QP problem using the primal active set method
QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer.Solution solution1 = solver1.solve(problem);
solution1.search(new DenseVector(2., 0.));
// print out the solution
System.out.println("minimizer = " + solution1.minimizer().minimizer());
System.out.println("minimum = " + solution1.minimum());
```

Again, we have *f*(1.4, 1.7) =  − 6.45\. You are encouraged to compare the output to the trace of iterations we discussed earlier.

#### 10.3.2.2 Dual Active-Set Method

The concept of duality is a technique to solve a problem related to the original problem that we refer to as the primal problem. The related problem is called the dual problem. The dual problem is one in which the parameters are the Lagrange multipliers of the primal. In the case where the number of inequality constraints is much greater than the dimension of ***x***, solving the dual problem to find the Lagrange multipliers and then finding ***x***^(***∗***) for the primal problem can be easier. Specifically, let ***x***^(***∗***),***λ***^(***∗***),***μ***^(***∗***) be the minimizer, the two Lagrange multipliers of a constrained optimization problem as in the KKT conditions. They solve the dual problem, as shown here:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\max}\mathcal{L}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu} \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgq.png)

subject to,

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}\nabla \mathcal{L}\left(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\mu} \right)=\mathbf{0}\\ {}\boldsymbol{\mu} \ge \mathbf{0}\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgr.png)

In addition, we have this:

![$$ f\left({\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}\right)=\mathcal{L}\left({\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast },{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}^{\ast },{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\ast}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgs.png)

The dual active-set method to solve the QP problem is essentially the active-set method in the previous section but applies to the dual of the QP problem. The dual of a QP problem is as follows:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\min }h\left(\boldsymbol{\mu} \right)=\frac{1}{2}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{A}{\boldsymbol{H}}^{-\mathbf{1}}{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\mu} -{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\left(\boldsymbol{A}{\boldsymbol{H}}^{-\mathbf{1}}\boldsymbol{p}+\boldsymbol{b}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgt.png)

subject to,

![$$ \boldsymbol{\mu} \boldsymbol{\ge}\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgu.png)

After its minimizer ***μ***^(**∗**) is determined, the minimizer of the primal problem can be obtained from the KKT conditions, as shown here:

![$$ \boldsymbol{Hx}+\boldsymbol{p}-{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{\mu} =\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgv.png)

That is,

![$$ {\boldsymbol{x}}^{\ast}={\boldsymbol{H}}^{-\mathbf{1}}\left({\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\ast}-\boldsymbol{p}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgw.png)

There are some advantages of solving the dual problem instead of the primal problem.

*   A feasible initial point can be readily identified as any vector with non-negative entries, e.g., ***μ***[**0**] ***=*** **0**.

*   The constraint matrix in the problem is the *p* × *p* identity matrix. Therefore, the dual problem always satisfies the nondegeneracy assumption.

*   The problem involves only bounded inequality constraints that significantly reduce the computation cost required in the algorithm.

In NM Dev, the class `QPDualActiveSetMinimizer` transforms a QP problem into its dual problem and then applies the active-set method. The following code uses the dual active-set method to solve the same problem:

```
// construct a quadratic function
Matrix H = new DenseMatrix(new double[][]{
{2, 0},
{0, 2}
});
Vector p = new DenseVector(new double[]{-2, -5});
QuadraticFunction f = new QuadraticFunction(H, p);
// construct the linear inequality constraints
Matrix A = new DenseMatrix(new double[][]{
{1, -2},
{-1, -2},
{-1, 2},
{1, 0},
{0, 1}
});
Vector b = new DenseVector(new double[]{-2, -6, -2, 0, 0});
LinearGreaterThanConstraints greater
= new LinearGreaterThanConstraints(A, b);// x >= 0
// construct the QP problem
QPProblem problem = new QPProblem(f, null, greater);
// construct a primal active set solver
double epsion = Math.sqrt(PrecisionUtils.autoEpsilon(problem.f().Hessian()));
QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer solver1
= new QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer(
epsion, // precision
Integer.MAX_VALUE // max number of iterations
);
// solve the QP problem using the primal active set method
QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer.Solution solution1 = solver1.solve(problem);
solution1.search(new DenseVector(2., 0.));
// print out the solution
System.out.println(solution1.minimizer().minimizer());
System.out.println(solution1.minimum());
// solve the QP problem using the dual active set method
QPDualActiveSetMinimizer solver2
= new QPDualActiveSetMinimizer(
epsion, // precision
Integer.MAX_VALUE); // max number of iterations
QPDualActiveSetMinimizer.Solution solution2 = solver2.solve(problem);
solution2.search();
// print out the solution
System.out.println("minimizer = " + solution2.minimizer().minimizer());
System.out.println("minimum = " + solution2.minimum());
```

We changed only the solver from this:

```
QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer solver1
= new QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer(
epsion, // precision
Integer.MAX_VALUE // max number of iterations
);
// solve the QP problem using the primal active set method
QPPrimalActiveSetMinimizer.Solution solution1 = solver1.solve(problem);
```

to

```
QPDualActiveSetMinimizer solver2
= new QPDualActiveSetMinimizer(
epsion, // precision
Integer.MAX_VALUE); // max number of iterations
QPDualActiveSetMinimizer.Solution solution2 = solver2.solve(problem);
```

We do not even need to provide an initial guess for the dual active-set solver.

The output is as follows:

## 10.4 Semidefinite Programming

Semidefinite programming (SDP) is a subfield of convex optimization concerned with the optimization of a linear objective function over the intersection of the cone of positive semidefinite matrices with an affine space. Positive semidefinite matrices are symmetric matrices whose eigenvalues are non-negative. SDP is a field of growing interest for several reasons. Many practical problems in operations research and combinatorial optimization can be modeled or approximated as SDP problems. In automatic control theory, SDP is used in the context of linear matrix inequalities. Some quantum query complexity problems have been formulated in terms of SDP. Moreover, all linear programs such as LP and QP can be reformulated as SDPs. The vector inequality constraints are replaced by matrix inequality constraints. Figure [10-13](#500382_1_En_10_Chapter.xhtml#Fig13) shows the hierarch of convex programming and subfields.

![../images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig13_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig13_HTML.png)

Figure 10-13

Hierarchy of convex programming

### 10.4.1 Primal and Dual SDP Problems

Let ***S***^(*n*) be the space of real symmetric *n* × *n* matrices . The standard inner product on ***S***^(*n*) is defined as follows:

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}\bullet \boldsymbol{B}=\mathrm{trace}\left(\boldsymbol{AB}\right)=\sum \limits_{i=1}^n\sum \limits_{j=1}^n{a}_{ij}{b}_{ij} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgx.png)

The primal SDP problem is defined as follows:

![$$ \min \boldsymbol{C}\bullet \boldsymbol{X} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equgy.png)

subject to,

***A***[*i*] ***∙ X = b***[*i*], for *i* = 1, 2, ..., *p*

***X*****≽ 0**

where ***C,X,A***[*i*] are in ***S***^(*n*). ***X*** is positive semidefinite.

A sample SDP problem looks like this:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{X}}{\min }{x}_{11}+2{x}_{12}+3{x}_{13}+2{x}_{21}+9{x}_{22}+0{x}_{23}+3{x}_{31}+0{x}_{32}+7{x}_{33}={x}_{11}+4{x}_{12}+6{x}_{13}+9{x}_{22}+7{x}_{33} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equha.png)

subject to,

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{x}_{11}+2{x}_{13}+3{x}_{22}+14{x}_{23}+5{x}_{33}=11\\ {}4{x}_{12}+16{x}_{13}+6{x}_{22}+4{x}_{33}=19\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhb.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{X}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{x}_{11}&amp; {x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{13}\\ {}{x}_{21}&amp; {x}_{22}&amp; {x}_{23}\\ {}{x}_{31}&amp; {x}_{32}&amp; {x}_{33}\end{array}\right]\succcurlyeq 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhc.png)

In matrix form, the problem is written as follows:

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{X}}{\min}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&amp; 2&amp; 3\\ {}2&amp; 9&amp; 0\\ {}3&amp; 0&amp; 7\end{array}\right]\bullet \left[\begin{array}{ccc}{x}_{11}&amp; {x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{13}\\ {}{x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{22}&amp; {x}_{23}\\ {}{x}_{13}&amp; {x}_{23}&amp; {x}_{33}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhd.png)

subject to,

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&amp; 0&amp; 1\\ {}0&amp; 3&amp; 7\\ {}1&amp; 7&amp; 5\end{array}\right]\bullet \left[\begin{array}{ccc}{x}_{11}&amp; {x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{13}\\ {}{x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{22}&amp; {x}_{23}\\ {}{x}_{13}&amp; {x}_{23}&amp; {x}_{33}\end{array}\right]=11\\ {}\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; 2&amp; 8\\ {}2&amp; 6&amp; 0\\ {}8&amp; 0&amp; 4\end{array}\right]\bullet \left[\begin{array}{ccc}{x}_{11}&amp; {x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{13}\\ {}{x}_{12}&amp; {x}_{22}&amp; {x}_{23}\\ {}{x}_{13}&amp; {x}_{23}&amp; {x}_{33}\end{array}\right]=19\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhe.png)

This SDP problem looks remarkably similar to an LP problem. Note that the decision variable involved now is a matrix ***X*** rather than a vector. Also, just as ***x*** ≥ **0** means that each of the *n* components must be non-negative, ***X*** **≽ 0** means that each of the *n* eigenvalues must be non-negative.

In NM Dev, the class `SDPPrimalProblem` constructs an SDP problem in primal form. The class signature is as follows:

```
public class SDPPrimalProblem { // TODO: convert to SDPDualProblem; implement ConstrainedOptimProblem
/**
* Constructs a primal SDP problem.
* \[
* \min_x \mathbf{c'x} \textrm{, s.t., } \\
* \mathbf{Ax} = \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{x} \geq \mathbf{0}
* \]
*
* @param C \(C\)
* @param A \(A\)
*/
public SDPPrimalProblem(SymmetricMatrix C, SymmetricMatrix[] A);
/**
* Gets the dimension of the system, i.e., the dimension of x, the
* number of variables.
*
* @return the dimension of the system
*/
public int n();
/**
* Gets the size of b.
*
* @return the size of b
*/
public int p();
/**
* Gets C.
*
* @return C
*/
public SymmetricMatrix C();
/**
* Gets Ai.
*
* @param i an index to the A's, counting from 1
* @return Ai
*/
public SymmetricMatrix A(int i);
}
```

The following code constructs the primal problem in the previous example:

```
// the primal SDP matrices
SymmetricMatrix C
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{1},
{2, 9},
{3, 0, 7}
});
SymmetricMatrix A1
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{1},
{0, 3},
{1, 7, 5}
});
SymmetricMatrix A2
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{0},
{2, 6},
{8, 0, 4}
});
// construct the primal SDP problem
SDPPrimalProblem primal
= new SDPPrimalProblem(
C,
new SymmetricMatrix[]{A1, A2}
);
```

If ***C =***  diag (***c***) and ***A***[***i***] ***=***  diag (***a***[***i***]) are all diagonal matrices, then the problem can be immediately reduced to a standard-form LP problem. The dual problem of a standard-form LP problem is as follows:

![$$ \max {\boldsymbol{b}}^{\boldsymbol{t}}\boldsymbol{y} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhf.png)

subject to,

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{y}+\boldsymbol{s}=\boldsymbol{c} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhg.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{s}\boldsymbol{\ge}\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhh.png)

where ***s*** is a slack variable.

Similarly, the dual SDP problem with respect to the primal SDP problem is as follows:

![$$ \max {\boldsymbol{b}}^{\boldsymbol{t}}\boldsymbol{y} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhi.png)

subject to,

![$$ \sum \limits_{i=1}^p{y}_i{\boldsymbol{A}}_i+\boldsymbol{S}=\boldsymbol{C} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhj.png)

***S*****≽ 0**

where ***S*** is a slack variable.

The dual problem of the example is as follows:

![$$ \max 11{y}_1+19{y}_2 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhl.png)

subject to,

![$$ {y}_1\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&amp; 0&amp; 1\\ {}0&amp; 3&amp; 7\\ {}1&amp; 7&amp; 5\end{array}\right]+{y}_2\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; 2&amp; 8\\ {}2&amp; 6&amp; 0\\ {}8&amp; 0&amp; 4\end{array}\right]+\boldsymbol{S}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1&amp; 2&amp; 3\\ {}2&amp; 9&amp; 0\\ {}3&amp; 0&amp; 7\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhm.png)

***S*****≽ 0**

Alternatively, it is as follows

![$$ \max 11{y}_1+19{y}_2 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equho.png)

subject to,

![$$ \left[\begin{array}{ccc}1-1{y}_1-0{y}_2&amp; 2-0{y}_1-2{y}_2&amp; 3-1{y}_1-8{y}_2\\ {}2-0{y}_1-2{y}_2&amp; 9-3{y}_1-6{y}_2&amp; 0-7{y}_1-0{y}_2\\ {}3-1{y}_1-8{y}_2&amp; 0-7{y}_1-0{y}_2&amp; 7-5{y}_1-4{y}_2\end{array}\right]\succcurlyeq \mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhp.png)

**≽ 0**

It is often easier to see and work with the dual form because the variables are the *p* multipliers, *y*[*i*]s.

The NM Dev class `SDPPrimalProblem` constructs an SDP problem in dual form. The class signature is as follows:

```
public class SDPDualProblem extends ConstrainedOptimProblemImpl1 {
/**
* Constructs a dual SDP problem.
*
* @param b \(b\)
* @param C \(C\)
* @param A \(A\)
*/
public SDPDualProblem(
final Vector b,
final SymmetricMatrix C,
final SymmetricMatrix[] A
);
/**
* Gets the dimension of the square matrices C and As.
*
* @return the dimension of the matrices
*/
public int n();
/**
* Gets the dimension of the system, i.e., p = the dimension of
* y, the number of
* variables.
*
* @return the dimension of the system
*/
public int p();
/**
* Gets b.
*
* @return b
*/
public ImmutableVector b();
/**
* Gets C.
*
* @return C
*/
public SymmetricMatrix C();
/**
* Gets Ai.
*
* @param i an index to the A's, counting from 1
* @return Ai
*/
public SymmetricMatrix A(int i);
}
```

Continuing with our example, the following code constructs the dual problem:

```
// the dual SDP vector and matrices
Vector b = new DenseVector(11., 19.);
// construct the primal SDP problem
SDPDualProblem dual
= new SDPDualProblem(
b,
C,
new SymmetricMatrix[]{A1, A2}
);
```

### 10.4.2 Central Path

The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions for an SDP problem say that matrix ***X***^(***∗***) is a minimizer of the primal problem if and only if there exists a matrix ***S***^(***∗***) ∈ ***S***^(*n*) and a vector ***y***^(***∗***) ∈ *ℝ*^(*p*) such that the following system holds:

![$$ \sum \limits_{i=1}^p{\boldsymbol{y}}_i^{\ast }{\boldsymbol{A}}_i+{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\ast }=\boldsymbol{C} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhq.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_i\bullet {\boldsymbol{X}}^{\ast }={b}_i $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhr.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{S}}^{\ast}{\boldsymbol{X}}^{\ast}=\mathbf{0} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhs.png)

X * ≽ 0, S* ≽ 0,

It can be shown that solution to the KKT conditions exists. The primal solution is ![$$ \left\{{\boldsymbol{X}}^{\ast},{\boldsymbol{y}}_i^{\ast},{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\ast}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq54.png). It can also be shown that ![$$ \left\{{\boldsymbol{y}}_i^{\ast},{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\ast}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq55.png) is then a maximizer, and hence a solution, for the dual problem. Therefore, this solution is called a primal-dual solution.

The central path plays an essential role in the construction of interior-point algorithms. For SDP problems, the central path consists of a set {***X***(*τ*), ***y***(*τ*), ***S***(*τ*)} such that the following system holds:

![$$ \sum \limits_{i=1}^p\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right){\boldsymbol{A}}_i+\boldsymbol{S}\left(\tau \right)=\boldsymbol{C} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhu.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_i\bullet \boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)={b}_i $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhv.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{S}\left(\tau \right)\boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)=\tau \boldsymbol{I} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhw.png)

X (τ) ≽ 0, S (τ) ≽ 0

It is almost a solution to the KKT conditions except for the *τ**I***.

This difference or duality gap, *δ*, along the central path can be evaluated as follows:

![$$ \delta \left[\boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right),\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right)\right]=\boldsymbol{C}\bullet \boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)-{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhy.png)

![$$ =\left[\sum \limits_{i=1}^p\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right){\boldsymbol{A}}_i+\boldsymbol{S}\left(\tau \right)\right]\bullet \boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)-{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equhz.png)

![$$ =\boldsymbol{S}\left(\tau \right)\boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)=\mathrm{trace}\left(\boldsymbol{S}\left(\tau \right)\boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)\right)=\mathrm{trace}\left(\tau \boldsymbol{I}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equia.png)

![$$ = n\tau $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equib.png)

If we can close the gap by tracing *τ* to 0, the central path approaches a solution to the SDP problem. See Figure [10-14](#500382_1_En_10_Chapter.xhtml#Fig14).

![../images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig14_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Fig14_HTML.jpg)

Figure 10-14

A central path for interior point algorithm

In other words,

![$$ \underset{\tau \to 0}{\lim}\delta \left[\boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right),\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right)\right]=0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equic.png)

Also, we have this:

![$$ \underset{\tau \to 0}{\lim}\boldsymbol{X}\left(\tau \right)={\boldsymbol{X}}^{\ast} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equid.png)

![$$ \underset{\tau \to 0}{\lim}\boldsymbol{y}\left(\tau \right)={\boldsymbol{y}}^{\ast} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equie.png)

![$$ \underset{\tau \to 0}{\lim}\boldsymbol{S}\left(\tau \right)={\boldsymbol{S}}^{\ast} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equif.png)

The primal-dual solution is ![$$ \left\{{\boldsymbol{X}}^{\ast},{\boldsymbol{y}}_{\boldsymbol{i}}^{\ast},{\boldsymbol{S}}^{\ast}\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq56.png).

Interior-point algorithms are developed to generate iterates that converge to a primal-dual solution by following the central path of the problem. For each *τ* > 0, ***X***(*τ*) and {***y***(*τ*), ***S***(*τ*)} are in the interior of the feasible region for the primal problem and the dual problem, respectively. Such is a path-following algorithm.

### 10.4.3 Primal-Dual Path-Following Method

We first define some operations and notations. Given matrices ***K***,***M***,***N*** in *ℝ*^(*n* × *n*), the general asymmetric Kronecker product is defined as follows:

![$$ \boldsymbol{M}\otimes \boldsymbol{N}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}{m}_{11}\boldsymbol{N}&amp; \dots &amp; {m}_{1n}\boldsymbol{N}\\ {}\mathbf{\vdots}&amp; \mathbf{\ddots}&amp; \mathbf{\vdots}\\ {}{m}_{n1}\boldsymbol{N}&amp; \dots &amp; {m}_{nn}\boldsymbol{N}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equig.png)

The operation svec(***K***) converts a symmetric matrix ***K =*** {*k*[*ij*]} into a vector of dimension *n*(*n* + 1)/2 as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{svec}\left(\boldsymbol{K}\right)={\left[{k}_{11},\sqrt{2}{k}_{12},\dots, \sqrt{2}{k}_{1n},{k}_{22},\sqrt{2}{k}_{23},\dots, \sqrt{2}{k}_{2n},\dots, {k}_{nn}\right]}^T $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equih.png)

The symmetric Kronecker product is defined by the identity, as shown here:

![$$ \left(\boldsymbol{M}\bigodot \boldsymbol{N}\right)\mathrm{svec}\left(\boldsymbol{K}\right)=\mathrm{svec}\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(\boldsymbol{NK}{\boldsymbol{M}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}+\boldsymbol{MK}{\boldsymbol{N}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equii.png)

For matrix variables, it is sometimes easier to represent and work with a matrix as a vector. The operation nevc(***K***) stacks the columns in ***K*** to create a vector.

In the Newton method, we start with a given set {***X***, ***y***, ***S***} and find increments ∆***X***, ∆***y***, ∆***S***, where ∆***X*** and ∆***S*** are symmetric, such that {∆***X***, ∆***y***, ∆***S***} satisfies the following linearized equations:

![$$ \sum \limits_{i=1}^p\Delta {\boldsymbol{y}}_i{\boldsymbol{A}}_i+\Delta \boldsymbol{S}=\boldsymbol{C}-\boldsymbol{S}-\sum \limits_{i=1}^p{\boldsymbol{y}}_i{\boldsymbol{A}}_i $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equij.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_i\bullet \Delta \boldsymbol{X}={b}_i-{\boldsymbol{A}}_i\bullet \boldsymbol{X} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equik.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{X}\Delta \boldsymbol{S}+\Delta \boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{X}+\Delta \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{S}+\boldsymbol{S}\Delta \boldsymbol{X}=2\tau \boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{XS}-\boldsymbol{SX} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equil.png)

The last equation can be expressed in terms of a symmetric Kronecker product:

![$$ \left(\boldsymbol{X}\bigodot \boldsymbol{I}\right)\mathrm{svec}\left(\Delta \boldsymbol{S}\right)+\left(\boldsymbol{S}\bigodot \boldsymbol{I}\right)\mathrm{svec}\left(\Delta \boldsymbol{X}\right)=\mathrm{svec}\left[\tau \boldsymbol{I}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{S}+\boldsymbol{SX}\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equim.png)

For simplicity, let’s denote the following:

![$$ \mathrm{svec}\left(\Delta \boldsymbol{X}\right)=\Delta \mathbf{x} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equin.png)

![$$ \mathrm{svec}\left(\Delta \boldsymbol{S}\right)=\Delta \mathbf{s} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equio.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{S}\bigodot \boldsymbol{I}=\boldsymbol{E} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equip.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{X}\bigodot \boldsymbol{I}=\boldsymbol{F} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equiq.png)

![$$ \mathrm{svec}\left[\tau \boldsymbol{I}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\boldsymbol{XS}+\boldsymbol{SX}\right)\right]={\boldsymbol{r}}_c $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equir.png)

The last equation in these notations becomes as follows:

![$$ \boldsymbol{E}\Delta \mathbf{x}+\mathbf{F}\Delta \mathbf{s}={\boldsymbol{r}}_c $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equis.png)

Furthermore, we let:

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}=\left[\begin{array}{c}{\left[\mathrm{svec}\left({\boldsymbol{A}}_1\right)\right]}^T\\ {}{\left[\mathrm{svec}\left({\boldsymbol{A}}_2\right)\right]}^T\\ {}\vdots \\ {}{\left[\mathrm{svec}\left({\boldsymbol{A}}_p\right)\right]}^T\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equit.png)

![$$ \mathbf{x}=\mathrm{svec}\left(\boldsymbol{X}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equiu.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{y}={\left[{y}_1,{y}_2,\dots, {y}_p\right]}^T $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equiv.png)

![$$ \Delta \boldsymbol{y}={\left[\Delta {y}_1,\Delta {y}_2,\dots, \Delta {y}_p\right]}^T $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equiw.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{r}}_p=\boldsymbol{b}-\boldsymbol{A}\mathbf{x} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equix.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{r}}_d=\mathrm{svec}\left(\boldsymbol{C}-\boldsymbol{S}-\mathrm{mat}\left({\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{y}\right)\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equiy.png)

where mat( ) is the inverse of svec( ).

With these notations, the linearized system can be written as follows:

![$$ \left\{\begin{array}{c}{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\Delta \boldsymbol{y}+\Delta \mathbf{s}={\boldsymbol{r}}_d\\ {}\boldsymbol{A}\Delta \mathbf{x}={\boldsymbol{r}}_p\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equiz.png)

Or in succent form, we have this:

![$$ \boldsymbol{J}\left[\begin{array}{c}\Delta \mathbf{x}\\ {}\Delta \boldsymbol{y}\\ {}\Delta \mathbf{s}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{\boldsymbol{r}}_d\\ {}{\boldsymbol{r}}_p\\ {}{\boldsymbol{r}}_c\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equja.png)

where:

![$$ \boldsymbol{J}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}\mathbf{0}&amp; {\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}&amp; \boldsymbol{I}\\ {}\boldsymbol{A}&amp; \mathbf{0}&amp; \mathbf{0}\\ {}\boldsymbol{E}&amp; \mathbf{0}&amp; \boldsymbol{F}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjb.png)

Antoniou & Lu (2007) provides the details of the interior point algorithm to solve the SDP problem as follows:

**Primal-Dual Path-Following Algorithm** **for SDP Problem**

**Step 1**

Input the problem as ***A***[*i*] for 1 ≤ *i* ≤ *p*, ***b*** ∈ *ℝ*^(*p*), ***C*** ∈ *ℝ*^(*n* × *n*), and a strictly feasible set {***X***[0], ***y***[0], ***S***[0]} that satisfies feasibility constraints and that ***X***[0] **≻** 0, ***S***[0] **≻** 0.

Choose a scalar *σ* ∈ [0, 1).

Set iteration counter *k* = 0 and initialize the tolerance ε for the duality gap *δ*[*k*].

**Step 2**

Compute the following:

![$$ {\delta}_k=\frac{{\boldsymbol{X}}_k\bullet {\boldsymbol{S}}_k}{n} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjc.png)

**Step 3**

If *δ*[*k*] ≤ ε, output the solution {***X***[***k***], ***y***[***k***], ***S***[***k***]} and stop.

Otherwise, set the following:

![$$ {\tau}_k=\sigma \frac{{\boldsymbol{X}}_k\bullet {\boldsymbol{S}}_k}{n} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjd.png)

**Step 4**

Solve the following:

![$$ \boldsymbol{J}\left[\begin{array}{c}\Delta \mathbf{x}\\ {}\Delta \boldsymbol{y}\\ {}\Delta \mathbf{s}\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{c}{\boldsymbol{r}}_d\\ {}{\boldsymbol{r}}_p\\ {}{\boldsymbol{r}}_c\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equje.png)

The solution is as follows:

![$$ \Delta \mathbf{x}=-{\boldsymbol{E}}^{-\mathbf{1}}\left[\boldsymbol{F}\left({\boldsymbol{r}}_d-{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\Delta \boldsymbol{y}\right)-{\boldsymbol{r}}_c\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjf.png)

![$$ \Delta \mathbf{s}={\boldsymbol{r}}_d-{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\Delta \boldsymbol{y} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjg.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{M}\Delta \boldsymbol{y}={\boldsymbol{r}}_p+\boldsymbol{A}{\boldsymbol{E}}^{-\mathbf{1}}\left(\boldsymbol{F}{\boldsymbol{r}}_d-{\boldsymbol{r}}_c\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjh.png)

where ***M*** is the Schur complement matrix given by the following:

![$$ \boldsymbol{M}=\boldsymbol{A}{\boldsymbol{E}}^{-\mathbf{1}}\boldsymbol{F}{\boldsymbol{A}}^{\boldsymbol{T}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equji.png)

Convert the solution {∆**x**, ∆***y***, ∆**s**} into {∆***X***, ∆***y***, ∆***S***} with ∆***X =*** mat(∆**x**) and ∆***S =*** mat(∆**s**).

**Step 5**

Choose a parameter *γ* ∈ (0, 1) and determine parameters *α* and *β* as follows:

![$$ \alpha =\min \left(1,\gamma \hat{\alpha}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjj.png)

![$$ \beta =\min \left(1,\gamma \hat{\beta}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjk.png)

where:

![$$ \hat{\alpha}=\underset{{\boldsymbol{X}}_k+\overline{\alpha}\Delta \boldsymbol{X}\ge 0}{\max}\overline{\alpha} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjl.png)

![$$ \hat{\beta}=\underset{{\boldsymbol{S}}_k+\overline{\beta}\Delta \boldsymbol{S}\ge 0}{\max}\overline{\beta} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjm.png)

**Step 6**

Set the following:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{X}}_{k+1}={\boldsymbol{X}}_k+\alpha \Delta \boldsymbol{X} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjn.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{y}}_{k+1}={\boldsymbol{y}}_k+\beta \Delta \boldsymbol{y} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjo.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{S}}_{k+1}={\boldsymbol{S}}_k+\beta \Delta \boldsymbol{S} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjp.png)

Set *k* = *k* + 1 and repeat from **step 2**.

Antoniou & Lu (2007) provides the following example. Find scalars *y*[1], *y*[2], *y*[3] such that the maximum eigenvalue of the following:

![$$ \boldsymbol{F}={\boldsymbol{A}}_{\mathbf{0}}+{y}_1{\boldsymbol{A}}_{\mathbf{1}}+{y}_2{\boldsymbol{A}}_{\mathbf{2}}+{y}_3{\boldsymbol{A}}_{\mathbf{3}} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjq.png)

is minimized.

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_0=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2&amp; -0.5&amp; -0.6\\ {}-0.5&amp; 2&amp; 0.4\\ {}-0.6&amp; 0.4&amp; 3\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjr.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_1=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; 1&amp; 0\\ {}1&amp; 0&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 0&amp; 0\end{array}\ \right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjs.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_2=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; 0&amp; 1\\ {}0&amp; 0&amp; 0\\ {}1&amp; 0&amp; 0\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjt.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_3=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; 0&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 0&amp; 1\\ {}0&amp; 1&amp; 0\end{array}\ \right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equju.png)

This problem can be formulated as a (dual) SDP problem.

![$$ \underset{\boldsymbol{y}}{\max }{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\boldsymbol{T}}\boldsymbol{y} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjv.png)

subject to,

![$$ \sum \limits_{i=1}^4{y}_i{\boldsymbol{A}}_i+\boldsymbol{S}=\boldsymbol{C} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjw.png)

S ≽ 0

And,

![$$ \boldsymbol{b}={\left[0\ 0\ 0\ 1\right]}^T $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjy.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{y}={\left[{y}_1\ {y}_2\ {y}_3\ {y}_4\right]}^T $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equjz.png)

![$$ \boldsymbol{C}=-{\boldsymbol{A}}_0 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equka.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{A}}_4=\boldsymbol{I} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equkb.png)

−*y*[4] is the maximum eigenvalue of matrix ***F***.

It is easy to verify that the initial set {***X***[0], ***y***[0], ***S***[0]} as follows:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{X}}_0=\frac{1}{3}\boldsymbol{I} $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equkc.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{y}}_0={\left[0.2\ 0.2\ 0.2-4\right]}^T $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equkd.png)

![$$ {\boldsymbol{S}}_0=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}2&amp; 0.3&amp; 0.4\\ {}0.3&amp; 2&amp; -0.6\\ {}0.4&amp; -0.6&amp; 1\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equke.png)

is strictly feasible for this primal-dual problem.

The matrix ***A*** is as follows:

![$$ \boldsymbol{A}=\left[\ \begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; \sqrt{2}&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 0&amp; \sqrt{2}\\ {}\begin{array}{c}0\\ {}1\end{array}&amp; \begin{array}{c}0\\ {}0\end{array}&amp; \begin{array}{c}0\\ {}0\end{array}\end{array}\kern1em \begin{array}{ccc}0&amp; 0&amp; 0\\ {}0&amp; 0&amp; 0\\ {}\begin{array}{c}0\\ {}1\end{array}&amp; \begin{array}{c}\sqrt{2}\\ {}0\end{array}&amp; \begin{array}{c}0\\ {}1\end{array}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equkf.png)

We set ![$$ \sigma =\frac{n}{15\sqrt{n}+n}=0.1035 $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_IEq57.png), *γ* = 0.9, *ε* = 0.001.

The algorithm, after four iterations, returns the solution {***X***^(***∗***), ***y***^(***∗***), ***S***^(***∗***)} where we have this:

![$$ {\boldsymbol{y}}^{\ast}=\left[\begin{array}{c}0.392921\\ {}0.599995\\ {}\begin{array}{c}-0.399992\\ {}-3.000469\end{array}\end{array}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_10_Chapter/500382_1_En_10_Chapter_TeX_Equkg.png)

The maximum eigenvalue of ***F*** is 3.

In NM Dev, the class `PrimalDualPathFollowingMinimizer` implements this primal-dual path-following algorithm. The following code solves the previous SDP problem:

```
// define an SDP problem with matrices and vectors
SymmetricMatrix A0
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{2},
{-0.5, 2},
{-0.6, 0.4, 3}
});
SymmetricMatrix A1
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{0},
{1, 0},
{0, 0, 0}
});
SymmetricMatrix A2
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{0},
{0, 0},
{1, 0, 0}
});
SymmetricMatrix A3
= new SymmetricMatrix(
new double[][]{
{0},
{0, 0},
{0, 1, 0}
});
SymmetricMatrix A4 = A3.ONE();
SymmetricMatrix C = A0.scaled(-1.);
Vector b = new DenseVector(0., 0., 0., 1.);
// construct an SDP problem
SDPDualProblem problem
= new SDPDualProblem(
b,
C,
new SymmetricMatrix[]{A1, A2, A3, A4});
// the initial feasible point
DenseMatrix X0
= new DenseMatrix(
new double[][]{
{1\. / 3., 0., 0.},
{0., 1\. / 3., 0.},
{0., 0., 1\. / 3.}
});
Vector y0 = new DenseVector(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, -4.);
DenseMatrix S0
= new DenseMatrix(
new double[][]{
{2, 0.3, 0.4},
{0.3, 2, -0.6},
{0.4, -0.6, 1}
});
// the initial central path
CentralPath path0 = new CentralPath(X0, y0, S0);
// solving SDP problem
PrimalDualPathFollowingMinimizer solver
= new PrimalDualPathFollowingMinimizer(
0.9, // γ
0.001); // ε
IterativeSolution solution = solver.solve(problem);
CentralPath path = solution.search(path0);
//the solution from the textbook is accurate up to epsilon
//changing epsilon will change the answers
// primal solution
System.out.println("X = ");
System.out.println(path.X);
// dual solution
System.out.println("y = ");
System.out.println(path.y);
System.out.println("S = ");
System.out.println(path.S);
```

The output is as follows:
