## 12.3 Probability Distribution

A probability distribution is a mathematical function that gives the probabilities of occurrence of different possible outcomes for an experiment. For example, the probability distribution of tossing a fair coin assigns 0.5 (50 percent) to heads and 0.5 (50 percent) to tails, respectively. A probability distribution is formally defined by a cumulative distribution function. The cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a real-valued random variable *X*, evaluated at *x*, is the probability that *X* will take a value less than or equal to *x*. Mathematically, it is:

![$$ {F}_X(x)=P\left(X\le x\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equam.png)

The CDF for tossing a fair coin, labeling heads as 0 and tails as 1, is a step-function, as shown here:

![$$ {F}_X(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}0.5,x=0\\ {}1,x=1\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equan.png)

See Figure [12-12](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig12).

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig12_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig12_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-12

Cumulative distribution function for fair coin toss

A random variable can be continuous, taking any numerical value in an interval or collection of intervals on the real line (having an uncountable range). Figure [12-13](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig13) shows a few CDFs for normal distributions. We see that for a normal distribution with *μ* = 0 (mean is 0), the chance of getting one sample from the probability distribution with a value smaller (or bigger) than 0 is 0.5.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig13_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig13_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-13

Cumulative distribution functions for the normal distributions

For a continuous random variable, it is often more intuitive to describe it using a probability density function (PDF).

![$$ {f}_X(x)=\frac{d}{dx}{F}_X(x) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equao.png)

*f*[*X*](*x*) is the relative likelihood that the random variable equals a sample value *x*. The bigger the relative likelihood, the more likely that we see this sample over another. The absolute likelihood is always 0 for a continuous random variable. Figure [12-14](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig14) shows the probability density functions for the cumulative distribution functions in Figure [12-13](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig13).

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig14_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig14_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-14

Probability density functions for the normal distributions

The probability that the value of a random variable falls within a certain region is the area of the region under the PDF, i.e., the integral of the PDF in the region. Mathematically, it is:

![$$ \mathrm{P}\left(a\le X\le b\right)={\int}_a^bf(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equap.png)

In particular, we have this (see Figure [12-15](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig15)):

![$$ {F}_X(x)=\mathrm{P}\left(-\infty &lt;X\le b\right)={\int}_{-\infty}^bf(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equaq.png)

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig15_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig15_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-15

The area under the probability density curve (left) is the value of the cumulative distribution function (right)

The quantile function of a probability distribution of a random variable specifies the value of the random variable such that the probability of the variable being less than or equal to that value equals the given probability. It is also called the inverse cumulative distribution function. Mathematically, the quantile function *Q* returns the value *x* such that:

![$$ {F}_X(x)=\mathrm{P}\left(X\le x\right)=u $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equar.png)

Or equivalently,

![$$ Q(p)=\operatorname{inf}\left\{x\in \mathbb{R}\ |\ u\le F(x)\right\} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equas.png)

*inf* is the infimum operator that gives the biggest element in the set that is smaller than or equal to all elements in the set, aka the greatest lower bound.

In general, almost surely, we have this:

![$$ Q\left(F(X)\right)=X $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equat.png)

Hence, we have the inverse cumulative distribution function. Here we capture the fact that the quantile function returns the minimum value of *x* from among all those values whose CDF value exceeds *u* (for continuous distributions).

In NM Dev, an implementation for a univariate probability function inherits from the `ProbabilityDistribution` interface. Such an implementation specifies not only the CDF and the PDF but also the descriptive statistics, e.g., mean and variance, of the distribution, among other information. The signature is as follows:

```
public interface ProbabilityDistribution {
/**
* Gets the mean of this distribution.
*
* @return the mean
* @see Wikipedia:
* Expected value
*/
public double mean();
/**
* Gets the median of this distribution.
*
* @return the media
* @see Wikipedia: Median
*/
public double median();
/**
* Gets the variance of this distribution.
*
* @return the variance
* @see Wikipedia:
* Variance
*/
public double variance();
/**
* Gets the skewness of this distribution.
*
* @return the skewness
* @see Wikipedia:
* Skewness
*/
public double skew();
/**
* Gets the excess kurtosis of this distribution.
*
* @return the excess kurtosis
* @see Wikipedia:
* Kurtosis
*/
public double kurtosis();
/**
* Gets the entropy of this distribution.
*
* @return the entropy
* @see
* Wikipedia:
* Entropy
* (information theory)
*/
public double entropy();
/**
* Gets the cumulative probability F(x) = Pr(X &le; x).
*
* @param x x
* @return F(x) = Pr(X &le; x)
* @see
* Wikipedia:
* Cumulative distribution function
*/
public double cdf(double x);
/**
* Gets the quantile, the inverse of the cumulative distribution function.
* It is the value below which random draws from the distribution would fall
* u&times;100 percent of the time.
* 
* F-1(u) = x, such that
* Pr(X &le; x) = u
* 
* This may not always exist.
*
* @param u {@code u}, a quantile
* @return F-1(u)
* @see Wikipedia:
* Quantile function
*/
public double quantile(double u);
/**
* The density function, which, if exists, is the derivative of F.
* It describes the density of probability at each point in the sample
* space.
* 
* f(x) = dF(X) / dx
* 
* This may not always exist.
* 
* For the discrete cases, this is the probability mass function. It gives
* the probability that a discrete random variable is exactly equal to some
* value.
*
* @param x x
* @return f(x)
* @see
* 
* Wikipedia:
* Probability density function
* Wikipedia:
* Probability
* mass function
* 
*/
public double density(double x);
/**
* The moment generating function is the expected value of
* etX. That is,
* 
* E(etX)
* 
* This may not always exist.
*
* @param t t
* @return E(exp(tX))
* @see
* Wikipedia:
* Moment-generating function
*/
public double moment(double t);
}
```

### 12.3.1 Moments

The mean or expected value of a probability distribution of a random variable *X*, denoted as E(*X*), is a generalization of the weighted sample mean or weighted average. For a discrete probability distribution, it is the weighted average with weights equal to the probability mass of the values.

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\sum \limits_{-\infty}^{\infty }x\mathrm{P}(x) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equau.png)

It is intuitively the arithmetic mean of a large number of independent realizations of *X*. The mean for a continuous probability distribution with PDF *f*(*x*) is defined as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\mu ={\int}_{-\infty}^{\infty } xf(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equav.png)

The mean may not exist or be finite. For some probability distributions, the mean is infinite (∞ or −∞), while for others the mean is undefined.

The variance of a probability distribution is defined as follows:

![$$ Var(X)={\sigma}^2={\int}_{-\infty}^{\infty }{\left(x-\mu \right)}^2f(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equaw.png)

![$$ ={\int}_{-\infty}^{\infty }{x}^2f(x) dx-{\mu}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equax.png)

In general, a standardized moment of a probability distribution is a moment (normally a higher-degree central moment) that is normalized. The normalization is typically a division by an expression of the standard deviation that renders the moment scale invariant. This has the advantage that such normalized moments differ only in other properties than variability so that the comparison of shape of different probability distributions is made easy. Mathematically, the standardized moment of degree *k* is defined as follows:

![$$ {\overset{\sim }{\mu}}_k=\frac{\mu_k}{\sigma^k} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equay.png)

where

![$$ {\mu}_k=\mathrm{E}\left[{\left(X-\mu \right)}^k\right]={\int}_{-\infty}^{\infty }{\left(x-\mu \right)}^kf(x) dx $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equaz.png)

and

![$$ {\sigma}^k={\left(\sqrt{\mathrm{E}\left[{\left(X-\mu \right)}^2\right]}\right)}^k $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equba.png)

Standardized moments are dimensionless numbers. The first standardized moment is zero, because the first moment about the mean is always zero. The second standardized moment is one, because the second moment about the mean is equal to the variance *σ*².

Skewness of a probability distribution, ![$$ \gamma ={\overset{\sim }{\mu}}_3 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq19.png), is the third standardized moment. It is a measure of the lopsidedness of the distribution. Any symmetric distribution will have a third central moment, if defined, of zero. A distribution that is skewed to the left (the tail of the distribution is longer on the left) will have a negative skewness. A distribution that is skewed to the right (the tail of the distribution is longer on the right) will have a positive skewness.

Kurtosis of a probability distribution, ![$$ \kappa ={\overset{\sim }{\mu}}_4 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq20.png), is the fourth standardized moment. It is a measure of the heaviness of the tail of the distribution, compared to the normal distribution of the same variance. Since it is the expectation of a fourth power, the fourth central moment, where defined, is always nonnegative; and except for a point distribution, it is always strictly positive and can be unbounded. If a distribution has heavy tails, the kurtosis will be high (called leptokurtic); conversely, thin-tailed distributions (for example, bounded distributions such as the uniform) have low kurtosis (called platykurtic).

The moment-generating function of a real-valued random variable is an alternative specification of its probability distribution. Like a probability density function or a cumulative distribution function, a moment-generating function, if it exists, also uniquely defines a probability distribution. As its name implies, the moment-generating function can be used to compute a distribution’s moments: the *n*-th moment about 0 is the *n*-th derivative of the moment-generating function, evaluated at 0\. Mathematically, the moment-generating function of a random variable *X* is defined as follows:

![$$ {M}_x(t)=\mathrm{E}\left[{e}^{tX}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbb.png)

That is, the function is an expectation of the random variable *e*^(*tX*) for *t* ∈ *ℝ*. The moment generation function does not exist if the integrals do not converge.

The moment-generating function is so named because it can be used to compute the moments of the distribution. Taylor’s expansion of *e*^(*tX*) gives the following:

![$$ {e}^{tX}=1+ tX+\frac{t^2{X}^2}{2!}+\frac{t^3{X}^3}{3!}+\cdots ++\frac{t^n{X}^n}{n!}+\cdots $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbc.png)

So, we have this:

![$$ {M}_x(t)=\mathrm{E}\left[{e}^{tX}\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbd.png)

![$$ =1+t\mathrm{E}(X)+\frac{t^2\mathrm{E}\left({X}^2\right)}{2!}+\frac{t^3\mathrm{E}\left({X}^3\right)}{3!}+\cdots ++\frac{t^n\mathrm{E}\left({X}^n\right)}{n!}+\cdots $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Eqube.png)

![$$ =1+t{m}_1+\frac{t^2{m}_2}{2!}+\frac{t^3{m}_3}{3!}+\cdots $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbf.png)

where *m*[*n*] is the *n*-th moment. Differentiating *M*[*x*](*t*) *i* times with respect to *t* and setting *t* = 0 gives the *i*-th moment about the origin *m*[*i*].

There are particularly simple results for the moment-generating functions of distributions defined by a linear transformation of random variables, if they exist. Specifically, if a random variable *X* has a moment-generating function *M*[*X*](*t*), then *αX* + *β* has the following moment-generating function:

![$$ {M}_{\alpha X+\beta }(t)=\mathrm{E}\left[{e}^{t\left( aX+\beta \right)}\right]={e}^{\beta t}{M}_X\left(\alpha t\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbg.png)

Moreover, if *S*[*n*] is a linear combination of random variables {*X*[*i*]} weighted by {*a*[*i*]}, as shown here:

![$$ {S}_n=\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{a}_i{X}_i $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbh.png)

then the moment-generating function for *S*[*n*] is as follows:

![$$ {M}_{S_n}(t)={M}_{X_1}\left({a}_1t\right){M}_{X_2}\left({a}_2t\right)\cdots {M}_{X_n}\left({a}_nt\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbi.png)

### 12.3.2 Normal Distribution

The most important distribution is (probably) the normal distribution or Gaussian distribution. Many natural processes such as heat diffusion are normally distributed. Moreover, the central limit theorem says that the average of many samples (observations) of a random variable with finite mean and variance is itself a random variable whose distribution converges to a normal distribution as the number of samples increases. Therefore, physical quantities that are the sum of many independent measurements, such as measurement errors, often have distributions that are nearly normal.

Mathematically, suppose {*X*[1], ⋯, *X*[*n*]} is a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables with E(*X*[*i*]) = *μ* and Var(*X*[*i*]) = *σ*² < ∞. Then as *n* goes to infinity, the random variable ![$$ \sqrt{n}\left({\overline{X}}_n-\mu \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq21.png) converges in distribution to a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance *σ*², i.e., *N*(0, *σ*²).

![$$ \sqrt{n}\left({\overline{X}}_n-\mu \right)\to N\left(0,{\sigma}^2\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbj.png)

A normal distribution mean *μ* and variance *σ*², denoted as *N*(*μ*, *σ*²), has a PDF as follows:

![$$ f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}\exp \left(-\frac{1}{2}{\left(\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma}\right)}^2\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbk.png)

Figure [12-16](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig16) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig16_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig16_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-16

Probability density functions for normal distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F(x)=\frac{1}{2}\left[1+\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma \sqrt{2}}\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbl.png)

Figure [12-17](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig17) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig17_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig17_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-17

Cumulative distribution functions for normal distributions

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\mu +\sigma \sqrt{2}{\operatorname{erf}}^{-1}\left(2q-1\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbm.png)

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\mu $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbn.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\mu $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbo.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbp.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbq.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=\exp \left(\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2{t}^2}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbr.png)

The NM Dev class `NormalDistribution` implements normal distribution. Here’s an example:

```
NormalDistribution dist = new NormalDistribution(
0., // mean
1\. // variance
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy()); // Math.log(2 * Math.PI * Math.E)
double[] xs = new double[]{
-1000000, -10000, -1000, -100, -10, -1, -0.1, -0.01, -0.001, -0.0001,
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.000001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

### 12.3.3 Log-Normal Distribution

A log-normal (or lognormal) distribution is a continuous probability distribution of a random variable whose logarithm is normally distributed. Thus, if the random variable *X* is log-normally distributed, then *Y* =  ln *X* has a normal distribution. Equivalently, if *Y* has a normal distribution, then the exponential function of *Y*, *X* =  exp (*Y*) has a log-normal distribution. A random variable that is log-normally distributed takes only positive real values. It is a convenient and useful model for measurements in exact and engineering sciences, as well as medicine, economics, and finance. The famous Black-Scholes model assumes that the stock returns are log-normally distributed.

Mathematically, a positive random variable *X* is log-normally distributed *X*~Lognormal(*μ*, *σ*²), if ln *X*~*N*(*μ*, *σ*²).

Let *φ*(*x*) and Φ(*x*) be the probability density function and the cumulative probability distribution function of the standard normal distribution *N*(0, 1). Then the PDF of *X*~Lognormal(*μ*, *σ*²) is as follows:

![$$ {f}_X(x)=\frac{d}{dx}\Pr \left(X\le x\right)=\frac{d}{dx}\Pr \left(\ln X\le \ln x\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbs.png)

![$$ =\frac{d}{dx}\Phi \left(\frac{\ln x-\mu }{\sigma}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbt.png)

![$$ =\frac{1}{x\sigma \sqrt{2\pi }}\exp \left(-\frac{{\left(\ln x-\mu \right)}^2}{2{\sigma}^2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbu.png)

Figure [12-18](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig18) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig18_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig18_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-18

Probability density functions for lognormal distributions; same ***μ*** but different ***σ***

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ {F}_X(x)=\Phi \left(\frac{\ln x-\mu }{\sigma}\right)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{erfc}\left(-\frac{\ln x-\mu }{\sigma \sqrt{2}}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbv.png)

erfc is a special function called the complementary error function.

Figure [12-19](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig19) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig19_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig19_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-19

Cumulative distribution functions for lognormal distributions; same ***μ*** but different ***σ***

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\exp \left(q+\sigma {Q}_{\Phi}(q)\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbw.png)

*Q*[Φ](*q*) is the quantile function of the standard normal distribution.

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\exp \left(\mu +\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbx.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\left[\exp \left({\sigma}^2\right)-1\right]\exp \left(2\mu +{\sigma}^2\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equby.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\left[\exp \left({\sigma}^2\right)+2\right]\sqrt{\exp \left({\sigma}^2\right)-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equbz.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\exp \left(4{\sigma}^2\right)+2\exp \left(3{\sigma}^2\right)+3\exp \left(2{\sigma}^2\right)-6 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equca.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=\exp \left(\mu t+\frac{\sigma^2{t}^2}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcb.png)

The NM Dev class `LogNormalDistribution` implements log-normal distribution. Here’s an example:

```
LogNormalDistribution dist = new LogNormalDistribution(
1., // mean
2\. // variance
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] xs = new double[]{
-1000000, -10000, -1000, -100, -10, -1, -0.1, -0.01, -0.001, -0.0001,
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.000001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

### 12.3.4 Exponential Distribution

A Poisson process is a model for a series of discrete events where the probability of an event happening is the same at any time or during any equal length time interval, but the exact timing of events is random. The arrival of an event, and hence the waiting time before the event happens, is independent of all the events and information before. The process is therefore said to be memoryless. For example, from historical data we know that the arrival of new customers is on average *λ* = 10 people per hour, but the timing of the next customer is completely random and is independent of any previous customers. The customer arrival process can be modeled as a Poisson process.

More abstractly, in Figure [12-20](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig20), a process starting at state 0 can jump to the next incremental state at a random time. We do not know when exactly it will happen as it is random. But we know that it can happen at any time with equal probability.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig20_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig20_HTML.png)

Figure 12-20

A Poisson point process starting from 0, in which increments occur continuously and independently at rate ***λ***

A Poisson process is defined as a random process such that the following holds:

1.  *N*(0) = 0.

2.  The increments {*N*(*t*[*n* + 1]) − *N*(*t*[*n*])} are independent random variables.

3.  The mean of the i.i.d. random increments is E(*N*(*t*[*n* + 1]) − *N*(*t*[*n*])) = *λ*(*t*[*n* + 1] − *t*[*n*]).

*λ*, called the intensity, is the expected number of arrivals that occurs per unit of time.

The random time between events or the random time before the next jump is called the waiting time . Its distribution is governed by the exponential distribution with the rate parameter *λ*.

Mathematically, a non-negative random variable *X* has exponential distribution *X*~Exp(*λ*) if and only if it has the following PDF:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ \lambda \right)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}\lambda {e}^{-\lambda x},x\ge 0\\ {}0,\kern0.5em x&lt;0\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcc.png)

Figure [12-21](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig21) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig21_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig21_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-21

Probability density functions for exponential distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F\left(x\ |\ \lambda \right)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}1-{e}^{-\lambda x},x\ge 0\\ {}0,\kern0.5em x&lt;0\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcd.png)

Figure [12-22](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig22) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig22_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig22_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-22

Cumulative distribution functions for exponential distributions

We can derive an important property of the exponential distribution called the memoryless property from the CDF. Specifically, here’s an example:

![$$ \Pr \left(T&gt;s+t\ |\ T&gt;s\right)=\frac{\Pr \left(T&gt;s+t\cap T&gt;s\right)}{\Pr \left(T&gt;s\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equce.png)

![$$ =\frac{\Pr \left(T&gt;s+t\ \right)}{\Pr \left(T&gt;s\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcf.png)

![$$ =\frac{e^{-\lambda \left(s+t\right)}}{e^{-\lambda s}}={e}^{-\lambda t} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcg.png)

![$$ =\Pr \left(T&gt;t\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equch.png)

*s* is irrelevant. When *T* is interpreted as the waiting time for an event to occur relative to some initial time, this relation implies that if *T* is conditioned on a failure to observe the event over some initial period of time *s*, the distribution of the remaining waiting time is the same as the original unconditional distribution. For example, if an event has not occurred after 30 seconds, the conditional probability that occurrence will take at least 10 more seconds is equal to the unconditional probability of observing the event more than 10 seconds after the initial time.

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=-\frac{\ln \left(1-q\right)}{\lambda } $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equci.png)

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\frac{1}{\lambda } $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcj.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\frac{1}{\lambda^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equck.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcl.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =6 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcm.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=\frac{\lambda }{\lambda -t},t&lt;\lambda $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcn.png)

The NM Dev class `ExponentialDistribution` implements the exponential distribution. Here’s an example:

```
ExponentialDistribution dist = new ExponentialDistribution(
1.0 // lambda = 1.
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());

System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());

-1000000, -10000, -1000, -100, -10, -1, -0.1, -0.01, -0.001, -0.0001,
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.000001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);

### 12.3.5 Poisson Distribution

While the waiting time between events of a Poisson process is governed by the exponential distribution, the number of events is governed by the Poisson distribution. In other words, a Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution that expresses the probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time if these events occur with a known constant mean rate and independently of the time since the last event. Note that unlike the other continuous probability distributions that we have discussed so far, Poisson distribution is a discrete probability distribution. It “counts” the number of event occurrences.

For instance, a call center receives an average of 180 calls per hour, 24 hours a day. The calls are independent; receiving one does not change the probability of when the next one will arrive. The number of calls received during any minute has a Poisson distribution: the most likely numbers are 2 and 3, but 1 and 4 are also likely, and there is a small probability of it being as low as zero and a very small probability it could be 10\. Another example is the number of decay events that occur from a radioactive source in a given observation period.

A discrete random variable *X* is said to have a Poisson distribution, with parameter *λ* > 0, if it has a probability mass function (PMF) given by the following:

![$$ f\left(k\ |\ \lambda \right)=\Pr \left(X=k\right)=\frac{\lambda^k{e}^{-\lambda }}{k!} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equco.png)

where *k* = 0, 1, 2, … is the number of occurrences.

For the example in Figure [12-23](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig23), *k* is the number of occurrences. *λ* is the expected rate of occurrences. The vertical axis is the probability of *k* occurrences given *λ*. The function is defined only at integer values of *k*; the connecting lines are only guides for the eye.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig23_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig23_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-23

Probability mass functions for Poisson distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F(k)={e}^{-\lambda}\sum \limits_{i=0}^{\underset{\_}{k}}\frac{\lambda^i}{i!} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcp.png)

![$$ \underset{\_}{k} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq22.png) is the floor function, the smallest integer smaller than or equal to *k*.

For the example in Figure [12-23](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig23), the horizontal axis is the index *k*, which is the number of occurrences. The CDF is discontinuous at the integers of *k* and flat everywhere else because a variable that is Poisson distributed takes on only integer values. See Figure [12-24](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig24).

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig24_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig24_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-24

Cumulative probability functions for Poisson distributions

There is no closed form for the quantile function, but it can be computed by a search for the biggest *k* using the CDF such that *F*(*k*) < *q*.

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\lambda $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcq.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\lambda $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcr.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma ={\lambda}^{-\frac{1}{2}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcs.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa ={\lambda}^{-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equct.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=\exp \left[\lambda \left({e}^t-1\right)\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcu.png)

The NM Dev class `PoissonDistribution` implements the Poisson distribution. Here’s an example:

```
PoissonDistribution dist = new PoissonDistribution(
2\. // lambda = 2.
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] ks = new double[]{
0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", k, dist.cdf(k)));
}
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", k, dist.density(k)));
}
for (double u = 0.1; u < 1d; u += 0.1) {
double x = dist.quantile(u);
System.out.println(String.format("Q(%f) = %f", u, x));
}
```

### 12.3.6 Binomial Distribution

The binomial distribution with parameters *n* and *p* is the discrete probability distribution of the number of successes in a sequence of *n* independent experiments, each with its own yes or no outcome: yes/success (with probability *p*) or no/failure (with probability *q* = 1 − *p*). A single success/failure experiment is also called a Bernoulli trial or Bernoulli experiment, and a sequence of Boolean outcomes is called a Bernoulli process. For a single trial, i.e., *n* = 1, the binomial distribution is a Bernoulli distribution. For one fair coin toss, *n* = 1, *p* = 0.5.

The binomial distribution is frequently used to model the number of successes in a sample of size *n* drawn with replacement from a population of size *N*. If the sampling is carried out without replacement, the draws are not independent and so the resulting distribution is a hypergeometric distribution, not a binomial one. However, for *N* much larger than *n*, the binomial distribution remains a good approximation and is widely used.

The binomial and Poisson distributions are similar in the sense that they both measure the number of certain random events (or “successes”) within a certain frame. However, they are different because the binomial distribution counts discrete occurrences among discrete trials, while the Poisson distribution counts discrete occurrences among a continuous domain. That is, with a binomial distribution you have a certain number, *n*, of “attempts,” each of which has probability of success *p*. With a Poisson distribution, you essentially have infinite attempts, with infinitesimal chance of success. That is, given a binomial distribution with parameters *n* and *p*, if you let *n* → ∞ and *p* → 0 in such a way that *np* → *λ*, then that distribution approaches a Poisson distribution with parameter *λ*. The Poisson distribution can therefore be derived as a limit of the binomial distribution.

Because of this limiting behavior, Poisson distributions are used to model rare occurrences of events that could happen a large number of times, but happen with a small probability. That is, they are used in situations that would be more properly represented by a binomial distribution with a very large *n* and small *p*, especially when the exact values of *n* and *p* are unknown, for example, a once-in-100-year flood.

In summary, if a mean or average probability of an event happening per unit time is given and you are asked to calculate a probability of *n* events happening in a given time, then the Poisson distribution is used. If, on the other hand, an exact probability of an event happening is given and you are asked to calculate the probability of this event happening *k* times out of *n*, then the binomial distribution should be used.

Moreover, if *n* is big enough, then the binomial random variable *X* can be well approximated by a normal distribution. That is, *X*~*N*(*np*, *np*(1 − *p*)). Equivalently, the normalized random variable ![$$ z=\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma } $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq23.png) has a standard normal distribution *N*(0, 1).

If the random variable *X* follows the binomial distribution with parameters *n* ∈ *ℕ* and *p* ∈ [0, 1], we write *X*~*B*(*n*, *p*). The probability of getting exactly *k* successes in *n* independent Bernoulli trials is given by the PMF:

![$$ f\left(k\ |\ n,p\right)=\Pr \left(k\ |\ n,p\right)=\Pr \left(X=k\right)=\left(\begin{array}{c}n\\ {}k\end{array}\right){p}^k{\left(1-p\right)}^{n-k} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcv.png)

for *k* = 0, 1, 2, …, *n*.

![$$ \left(\begin{array}{c}n\\ {}k\end{array}\right)=\frac{n!}{k!\left(n-k\right)!} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq24.png) is the binomial coefficient, which is the reason for the name of the distribution. The formula can be understood as follows: *k* successes occur with probability *p*^(*k*), and *n* − *k* failures occur with probability (1 − *p*)^(*n* − *k*). However, the *k* successes can occur anywhere among the *n* trials, and there are ![$$ \left(\begin{array}{c}n\\ {}k\end{array}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq25.png) different ways of distributing *k* successes in a sequence of *k* trials.

Figure [12-25](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig25) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig25_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig25_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-25

Probability mass functions for binomial distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F\left(k\ |\ n,p\right)=\Pr \left(X\le k\right)=\sum \limits_{i=0}^{\underset{\_}{k}}\left(\begin{array}{c}n\\ {}i\end{array}\right){p}^i{\left(1-p\right)}^{n-i} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcw.png)

Figure [12-26](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig26) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig26_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig26_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-26

Cumulative probability functions for binomial distributions

There is no closed form for the quantile function, but it can be computed by a search for the biggest *k* using the CDF such that *F*(*k*) < *q*.

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)= np $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcx.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)= npq $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcy.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\frac{q-p}{\sqrt{npq}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equcz.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\frac{1-6 pq}{npq} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equda.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)={\left(q+p{e}^t\right)}^n $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdb.png)

The NM Dev class `BinomialDistribution` implements the binomial distribution. Here’s an example:

```
BinomialDistribution dist = new BinomialDistribution(
20, // n
0.7 // p
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] ks = DoubleUtils.seq(0., 20., 1.); // a sequence of numbers from 0 to 20
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", k, dist.cdf(k)));
}
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", k, dist.density(k)));
}
for (double u = 0.1; u < 1d; u += 0.1) {
double x = dist.quantile(u);
System.out.println(String.format("Q(%f) = %f", u, x));
}
```

### 12.3.7 T-Distribution

The student’s t-distribution (or simply the t-distribution) is the probability distribution of the sample mean relative to the true mean of a sample of i.i.d. normally distributed population when the sample size is small and the population’s standard deviation is unknown. Specifically, suppose the set {*x*[1], …, *x*[*n*]} is drawn from a normal distribution with known mean *μ* and unknown variance; then the t-value, a standardized value, of such a sample is defined as follows:

![$$ t=\frac{\overline{x}-\mu }{s/\sqrt{n}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdc.png)

where ![$$ \overline{x} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq26.png) is the sample mean and *s* is the unbiased sample standard deviation (with the denominator *n* − 1) in place of the true population standard deviation *σ*. *t* is random because ![$$ \overline{x} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq27.png) and *s* are random. The random variable *t* has the t-distribution with *υ* = *n* − 1 degrees of freedom.

The t-distribution plays a role in a number of widely used statistical analyses including student’s t-test for assessing the statistical significance of the difference between two sample means (whether two means are significantly different statistically), in the construction of confidence intervals for the difference between two population means, and in linear regression analysis. The student’s t-distribution also arises in the Bayesian analysis of data from a normal family.

Mathematically, a random variable *X* has the t-distribution if and only if it has the PDF as shown here:

![$$ f(t)=\frac{\Gamma \left(\frac{\upsilon +1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{\upsilon \pi}\Gamma \left(\frac{\upsilon }{2}\right)}{\left(1+\frac{t^2}{\upsilon}\right)}^{-\frac{\upsilon +1}{2}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdd.png)

where *υ* is the number of degree of freedom and Γ the gamma function.

Figure [12-27](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig27) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig27_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig27_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-27

T-distributions (red) versus normal distributions (blue)

The t-distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, like the normal distribution. However, the t-distribution has heavier tails, meaning that it is more prone to producing values that fall far from its mean. When the degree of freedom goes to infinity, the t-distribution converges to normal distribution. That is,

![$$ \underset{\upsilon \to \infty }{\lim }t=\frac{\overline{x}-\mu }{\sigma /\sqrt{n}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equde.png)

This has a standard normal distribution with mean 0 and variance 1.

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F(t)=1-\frac{1}{2}{I}_{x(t)}\left(\frac{\nu }{2},\frac{1}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdf.png)

where *I* is the the regularized incomplete beta function, *t* > 0, and we have this:

![$$ x(t)=\frac{\nu }{t^2+\nu } $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdg.png)

Figure [12-28](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig28) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig28_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig28_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-28

Cumulative probability functions for t-distributions

The quantile function for the t-distribution has simple formulas when the degree of freedom *υ* = 1, 2, 4\. They are as follows:

![$$ \upsilon =1, $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdh.png)

![$$ Q(q)=\tan \left(\pi \left(q-\frac{1}{2}\right)\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdi.png)

![$$ \upsilon =2, $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdj.png)

![$$ Q(q)=2\left(q-\frac{1}{2}\right)\sqrt{\frac{2}{\alpha }} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdk.png)

![$$ \alpha =4q\left(1-q\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdl.png)

![$$ \upsilon =4, $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdm.png)

![$$ Q(q)=\operatorname{sign}\left(q-\frac{1}{2}\right)2\sqrt{u-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdn.png)

![$$ u=\frac{\cos \left(\frac{1}{3}{\cos}^{-1}\sqrt{\alpha}\right)}{\sqrt{\alpha }} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdo.png)

The sign function returns 1 for a positive number, -1 for a negative number, and 0 otherwise.

In general, the quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\operatorname{sign}\left({I}^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\frac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{4\nu {\left({I}^{-1}-\frac{1}{2}\right)}^2}-\frac{1}{\nu }}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdp.png)

![$$ {I}^{-1}={I}_{\left(\frac{\nu }{2},\frac{\nu }{2}\right)}^{-1}(q) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq28.png) is the inverse of the regularized incomplete Beta function with both shape parameters being ![$$ \frac{\nu }{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq29.png).

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdq.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\left\{\begin{array}{c}\infty, 1&lt;\nu \le 2\\ {}\frac{\nu }{\nu -2},\nu &gt;2\kern0.5em \end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq30.png), otherwise undefined

The skewness is as follows:

*γ* = 0, *ν* > 3, otherwise undefined

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\left\{\begin{array}{c}\infty, 2&lt;\nu \le 4\\ {}\frac{6}{\nu -4},\nu &gt;4\end{array}\right. $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq31.png), otherwise undefined

The moment-generating function is undefined.

The NM Dev class `TDistribution` implements the t-distribution. Here’s an example:

```
TDistribution dist = new TDistribution(4.5); // degree of freedom = 4.5
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] ks = DoubleUtils.seq(0., 20., 1.); // a sequence of numbers from 0 to 20
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", k, dist.cdf(k)));
}
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", k, dist.density(k)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.1; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

The output is as follows:

### 12.3.8 Chi-Square Distribution

While the scaled sample mean, a sum of *k* independent normal random variables, follows the t-distribution, a sum of the squares of *k* independent standard normal random variables follows the Chi-square distribution (also χ²-distribution). This distribution is sometimes called the central Chi-square distribution, a special case of the more general noncentral Chi-square distribution. The Chi-square distribution is one of the most widely used probability distributions in inferential statistics, notably in hypothesis testing and in the construction of confidence intervals. It is also used in the common Chi-square tests for goodness of fit of an observed distribution to a theoretical one. See Section 12.4.

Mathematically, if each variable in {*Z*[1], …, *Z*[*k*]} is an independent, standard normal random variable, then the sum of their squares, as shown here:

![$$ Q=\sum \limits_{i=1}^k{Z}_i^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdr.png)

has the Chi-square distribution *k* degrees of freedom. This is usually denoted as *Q*~*χ*²(*k*) or ![$$ Q\sim {\chi}_k^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq32.png). The Chi-square distribution has one parameter: a positive integer *k* that specifies the degree of freedom (the number of random variables being summed, *Z*[*i*] s).

Moreover, the sample variance *S*² has the scaled Chi-square distribution.

![$$ {S}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{\left({x}_i-\overline{x}\right)}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equds.png)

![$$ {S}^2\sim \frac{\sigma^2}{n-1}{\chi}_{n-1}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdt.png)

Equivalently, we have this:

![$$ \frac{S^2}{\sigma^2}\sim \frac{\chi_{n-1}^2}{n-1} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdu.png)

The PDF of the Chi-square distribution is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ k\right)=\frac{x^{\frac{k}{2}-1}{e}^{-\frac{x}{2}}}{2^{\frac{k}{2}}\Gamma \left(\frac{k}{2}\right)},x&gt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdv.png)

where ![$$ \Gamma \left(\frac{k}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq33.png) is the gamma function.

Figure [12-29](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig29) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig29_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig29_HTML.png)

Figure 12-29

Probability density functions for Chi-square distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F\left(x\ |\ k\right)=\frac{\gamma \left(\frac{k}{2},\frac{x}{2}\right)}{\Gamma \left(\frac{k}{2}\right)}=P\left(\frac{k}{2},\frac{x}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdw.png)

where *γ*(*s*, *t*) is the lower incomplete gamma function, and *P*(*s*, *t*) is the regularized incomplete gamma function.

Figure [12-30](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig30) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig30_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig30_HTML.png)

Figure 12-30

Cumulative distribution functions for Chi-square distributions

The quantile function is the inverse of the regularized incomplete gamma function.

![$$ Q(q)={P}^{-1}\left(\frac{k}{2},\frac{q}{2}\right)=2{P}^{-1}\left(\frac{k}{2},q\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdx.png)

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=k $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdy.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=2k $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equdz.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\sqrt{\frac{8}{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equea.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\frac{12}{k} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equeb.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)={\left(1-2t\right)}^{-\frac{k}{2}},t&lt;\frac{1}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equec.png)

The NM Dev class `ChiSquareDistribution` implements the Chi-square distribution. Here’s an example:

```
ChiSquareDistribution dist = new ChiSquareDistribution(
1.5 // degree of freedom
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] xs = new double[]{
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.1; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

The output is as follows:

```
mean = 1.5
median = 1.5
variance = 3.0
skew = 2.309401076758503
kurtosis = 8.0
entropy = 1.3749629120446232
F(0.000000) = 0.000000

f(0.000000) = Infinity

### 12.3.9 F-Distribution

While the scaled sample mean, namely, the t-value, has the t-distribution, the ratio of the scaled sample variances has the F-distribution. In fact, the ratio of a random variable that has a Chi-square distribution with the degree of freedom *d*[1] over another random variable that has a Chi-square distribution with the degree of freedom *d*[2] follows the F-distribution with the degrees of freedom (*d*[1], *d*[2]), *F*(*d*[1], *d*[2]). That is,

![$$ \frac{\chi_{d_1}^2}{\chi_{d_2}^2}\sim F\left({d}_1,{d}_2\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equed.png)

Moreover, the sample variance *S*² has Chi-square distribution.

![$$ {S}^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{\left({x}_i-\overline{x}\right)}^2\sim \frac{\sigma^2}{n-1}{\chi}_{n-1}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equee.png)

Then the ratio of the sample variances of two samples ![$$ \frac{S_1^2}{S_2^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq34.png) and the ratio of the scaled sample variances ![$$ \frac{S_1^2/{\sigma}_1^2}{S_2^2/{\sigma}_2^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq35.png) follow the F-distribution. Moreover, for the random variable *t* with the degree of freedom *ν*, *t*² has the F-distribution *F*(1, *ν*).

If a random variable *X* has an F-distribution with parameters *d*[1] > 0 and *d*[2] > 0, we write *X*~*F*(*d*[1], *d*[2]). The PDF is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ {d}_1,{d}_2\right)=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{{\left({d}_1x\right)}^{d_1}{d_2}^{d_2}}{{\left({d}_1x+{d}_2\right)}^{d_1+{d}_2}}}}{xB\left(\frac{d_1}{2},\frac{d_2}{2}\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equef.png)

*B* is the beta function.

Figure [12-31](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig31) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig31_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig31_HTML.png)

Figure 12-31

Probability density functions for F-distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F\left(x\ |\ {d}_1,{d}_2\right)={I}_{\frac{d_1x}{d_1x+{d}_2}}\left(\frac{d_1}{2},\frac{d_2}{2}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equeg.png)

*I* is the regularized incomplete beta function.

Figure [12-32](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig32) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig32_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig32_HTML.png)

Figure 12-32

Cumulative distribution functions for F-distributions

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\frac{d_2{I}^{-1}}{d_1-{d}_1{I}^{-1}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equeh.png)

![$$ {I}^{-1}={I}_{\left(\frac{d_1}{2},\frac{d_2}{2}\right)}^{-1}(q) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq36.png) is the inverse of the regularized incomplete Beta functions with the shape parameters ![$$ \frac{d_1}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq37.png) and ![$$ \frac{d_2}{2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq38.png).

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\frac{d_2}{d_2-2},{d}_2&gt;2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equei.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\frac{2{d}_2^2\left({d}_1+{d}_2-2\right)}{d_1{\left({d}_2-2\right)}^2\left({d}_2-4\right)},{d}_2&gt;4 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equej.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\frac{\left(2{d}_1+{d}_2-2\right)\sqrt{8\left({d}_2-4\right)}}{\left({d}_2-6\right)\sqrt{d_1\left({d}_1+{d}_2-2\right)}},{d}_2&gt;6 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equek.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =12\frac{d_1\left(5{d}_2-22\right)\left({d}_1+{d}_2-2\right)+\left({d}_2-4\right){\left({d}_2-2\right)}^2}{d_1\left({d}_2-6\right)\left({d}_2-8\right)\left({d}_1+{d}_2-2\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equel.png)

The moment-generating function for F-distribution does not exist.

The NM Dev class `FDistribution` implements F-distribution. Here’s an example:

```
FDistribution dist = new FDistribution(100.5, 10); // degrees of freedom = {100.5, 10}
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
double[] ks = DoubleUtils.seq(0., 20., 1.); // a sequence of numbers from 0 to 20
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", k, dist.cdf(k)));
}
for (double k : ks) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", k, dist.density(k)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.1; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

### 12.3.10 Rayleigh Distribution

The Rayleigh distribution is a continuous probability distribution for non-negative-valued random variables. It is essentially a Chi-square distribution with two degrees of freedom. For example, ![$$ X=\sqrt{X_1^2+{X}_2^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq39.png) follows the Rayleigh distribution, where *X*[1] and *X*[2] are two normal distributions, and ![$$ {X}_1^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq40.png) and ![$$ {X}_2^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq41.png) are two Chi-square distributions.

A Rayleigh distribution is often observed when the overall magnitude of a vector is related to its directional components. One example where the Rayleigh distribution naturally arises is when wind velocity is analyzed in two dimensions. Assuming that each component is uncorrelated, normally distributed with equal variance, and zero mean, then the overall wind speed (vector magnitude) will be characterized by a Rayleigh distribution. A second example of the distribution arises in the case of random complex numbers whose real and imaginary components are independently and identically normally distributed with equal variance and zero mean. In that case, the absolute value of the complex number is Rayleigh-distributed.

Another possibility is that ![$$ X=\sigma \sqrt{-2\ln U} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq42.png), where *U* is a uniform distributed random variable, has a Rayleigh distribution with parameters *σ*.

The PDF is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ \sigma \right)=\frac{x}{\sigma^2}\exp \left(-\frac{x^2}{2{\sigma}^2}\right),x\ge 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equem.png)

where *σ* is the scale parameter of the distribution.

Figure [12-33](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig33) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig33_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig33_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-33

Probability density functions for Rayleigh distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F\left(x\ |\ \sigma \right)=1-\exp \left(-\frac{x^2}{2{\sigma}^2}\right),x\ge 0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equen.png)

Figure [12-34](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig34) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig34_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig34_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-34

Cumulative distribution functions for Rayleigh distributions

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\sigma \sqrt{-2\ln \left(1-q\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equeo.png)

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\sigma \sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equep.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\frac{4-\pi }{2}{\sigma}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equeq.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}\left(\pi -3\right)}{{\left(4-\pi \right)}^{\frac{3}{2}}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equer.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =-\frac{6{\pi}^2-24\pi +16}{{\left(4-\pi \right)}^2} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Eques.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=1+\sigma t\exp \left(\frac{\sigma^2{t}^2}{2}\right)\sqrt{\frac{\pi }{2}}\left(\operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{\sigma t}{\sqrt{2}}\right)+1\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equet.png)

The NM Dev class `RayleighDistribution` implements the Rayleigh distribution. Here’s an example:

```
RayleighDistribution dist = new RayleighDistribution(
2 // sigma = 2
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("median = " + dist.median());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] xs = new double[]{
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.000001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

### 12.3.11 Gamma Distribution

The gamma distribution is a two-parameter family of continuous probability distributions. The exponential distribution and Chi-square distribution are special cases of the gamma distribution. There are two different parameterizations in common use:

*   With a shape parameter *k* > 0 and a scale parameter *θ* > 0

*   With a shape parameter *α* = *k* > 0 and an inverse scale parameter ![$$ \beta =\frac{1}{\theta }&gt;0 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq43.png), called a rate parameter

The parameterization with *k* and *θ* appears to be more common in econometrics and certain other applied fields, where for example the gamma distribution is frequently used to model waiting times. For instance, the waiting time until failure is a random variable that is frequently modeled with a gamma distribution. NM Dev uses this parameterization with *k* and *θ*.

The parameterization with *α* and *β* is more common in Bayesian statistics, where the gamma distribution is used as a conjugate prior distribution for various types of inverse scale (rate) parameters, such as the *λ* of an exponential distribution or a Poisson distribution or, for that matter, the *β* of the gamma distribution itself.

A random variable *X* has the gamma distribution with shape *k*, and scale *θ* is denoted by the following:

![$$ X\sim \Gamma \left(k,\theta \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equeu.png)

The PDF is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ k,\theta \right)=\frac{x^{k-1}\exp \left(-\frac{x}{\theta}\right)}{\theta^k\Gamma (k)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equev.png)

where Γ(*k*) is the Gamma function evaluated at *k*.

Figure [12-35](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig35) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig35_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig35_HTML.png)

Figure 12-35

Probability density functions for Gamma distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ k,\theta \right)=\frac{\gamma \left(k,\frac{x}{\theta}\right)}{\Gamma (k)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equew.png)

Figure [12-36](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig36) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig36_HTML.png](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig36_HTML.png)

Figure 12-36

Cumulative distribution functions for Gamma distributions

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\theta {P}^{-1}\left(k,q\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equex.png)

where *P*^(−1) is the inverse of the regularized incomplete gamma function.

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)= k\theta $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equey.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=k{\theta}^2 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equez.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\frac{2}{k} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfa.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\frac{6}{k} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfb.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)={\left(1-\theta t\right)}^{-k},t&lt;\frac{1}{\theta } $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfc.png)

The NM Dev class `GammaDistribution` implements the Gamma distribution. Here’s an example:

```
GammaDistribution dist = new GammaDistribution(
1., // k = 1
2\. // theta = 2
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
double[] xs = new double[]{
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3, 10, 100, 1000};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

### 12.3.12 Beta Distribution

The beta distribution is a family of continuous probability distributions defined on the unit interval [0, 1] parameterized by two positive shape parameters *α* and *β*, which appear as exponents of the random variable and control the shape of the distribution. The beta distribution has been applied to model the behavior of random variables limited to intervals of finite length in a wide variety of disciplines. In Bayesian inference, the beta distribution is the conjugate prior probability distribution for the Bernoulli, binomial, negative binomial, and geometric distributions. The beta distribution is a suitable model for the random behavior of percentages and proportions.

A random variable *X* that has the beta distribution with parameters *α* and *β* is denoted by the following:

![$$ X\sim \mathrm{Beta}\left(\alpha, \beta \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfd.png)

The PDF is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ \alpha, \beta \right)=\frac{1}{\mathrm{B}\left(\alpha, \beta \right)}{x}^{\alpha -1}{\left(1-x\right)}^{\beta -1} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfe.png)

where B(*α*, *β*) is the beta function.

Figure [12-37](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig37) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig37_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig37_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-37

Probability density functions for Beta distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ \alpha, \beta \right)=\frac{\mathrm{B}\left(x\ |\ \alpha, \beta \right)}{\mathrm{B}\left(\alpha, \beta \right)}={I}_x\left(\alpha, \beta \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equff.png)

where B(*x* | *α*, *β*) is the incomplete beta function and *I*[*x*](*α*, *β*) is the regularized incomplete beta function.

Figure [12-38](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig38) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig38_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig38_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-38

Cumulative distribution functions for Beta distributions

The quantile function is the inverse of regularized incomplete beta function.

![$$ Q(q)={I}_q^{-1}\left(\alpha, \beta \right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfg.png)

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\frac{\alpha }{\alpha +\beta } $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfh.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\frac{\alpha \beta}{{\left(\alpha +\beta \right)}^2\left(\alpha +\beta +1\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfi.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\frac{2\left(\beta -\alpha \right)\sqrt{\alpha +\beta +1}}{\left(\alpha +\beta +2\right)\sqrt{\alpha \beta}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfj.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\frac{6\left[{\left(\alpha -\beta \right)}^2\left(\alpha +\beta +1\right)-\alpha \beta \left(\alpha +\beta +2\right)\right]}{\alpha \beta \left(\alpha +\beta +1\right)\left(\alpha +\beta +3\right)} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfk.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=1+\sum \limits_{k=1}^{\infty}\left(\prod \limits_{r=0}^{k-1}\frac{\alpha +r}{a+\beta +r}\right)\frac{t^k}{k!} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfl.png)

The NM Dev class `BetaDistribution` implement s the Beta distribution. Here’s an example:

```
BetaDistribution dist = new BetaDistribution(
0.5, // alpha = 0.5
1.5 // beta = 1.5
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
double[] xs = new double[]{
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

The output is as follows:

```
mean = 0.25
variance = 0.0625
skew = 1.0
kurtosis = 0.0
F(0.000000) = 0.000000
F(0.000100) = 0.012732
F(0.001000) = 0.040257
F(0.010000) = 0.127111
F(0.100000) = 0.395819
F(1.000000) = 1.000000
F(2.000000) = NaN
F(3.000000) = NaN
f(0.000000) = Infinity
f(0.000100) = 63.658794
f(0.001000) = 20.121616
f(0.010000) = 6.334287
f(0.100000) = 1.909859
f(1.000000) = 0.000000
f(2.000000) = NaN
f(3.000000) = NaN
F(Q(u)) = u for all u = true
```

Notice that the distribution is not defined outside the unit interval [0, 1] and that the probability density goes to infinity at *x* = 0.

### 12.3.13 Weibull Distribution

A non-negative random variable has the Weibull distribution with shape parameters *λ* > 0 and *k* > 0 if it has the following PDF:

![$$ f\left(x\ |\ \lambda, k\right)=\frac{k}{\lambda }{\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)}^{k-1}\exp \left(-{\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)}^k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfm.png)

Figure [12-39](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig39) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig39_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig39_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-39

Probability density functions for Weibull distributions

The CDF is as follows:

![$$ F\left(x\ |\ \lambda, k\right)=1-\exp \left(-{\left(\frac{x}{\lambda}\right)}^k\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfn.png)

Figure [12-40](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig40) shows an example.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig40_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig40_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-40

Cumulative distribution functions for Weibull distributions

The quantile function is as follows:

![$$ Q(q)=\lambda {\left(-\ln \left(1-q\right)\right)}^{\frac{1}{k}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfo.png)

The mean is as follows:

![$$ \mathrm{E}(X)=\lambda \Gamma \left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfp.png)

Γ is the gamma function.

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)={\lambda}^2\left[\Gamma \left(1+\frac{1}{2}\right)-{\left(\Gamma \left(1+\frac{1}{k}\right)\right)}^2\right] $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfq.png)

The skewness is as follows:

![$$ \gamma =\frac{\lambda^3\Gamma \left(1+\frac{3}{k}\right)-3\mu {\sigma}^2-{\mu}^3}{\sigma^3} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfr.png)

The excess kurtosis is as follows:

![$$ \kappa =\frac{\lambda^4\Gamma \left(1+\frac{4}{k}\right)-4\gamma {\sigma}^3\mu -6{\mu}^2{\sigma}^2-{\mu}^4}{\sigma^4}-3 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfs.png)

The moment-generating function is as follows:

![$$ {M}_X(t)=\sum \limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^n{\lambda}^n}{n!}\Gamma \left(1+\frac{n}{k}\right),k\ge 1 $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equft.png)

The NM Dev class `WeibullDistribution` implements the Weibull distribution. Here’s an example:

```
WeibullDistribution dist = new WeibullDistribution(
1, // lambda, the scale parameter = 1
1 // the shape parameter = 1
);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
System.out.println("entropy = " + dist.entropy());
double[] xs = new double[]{
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.001; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

The output is as follows:

```

variance = 1.0
skew = 1.9999999999999973
kurtosis = 6.0000000000000036
entropy = 1.0
F(0.000000) = 0.000000
F(0.000100) = 0.000100
F(0.001000) = 0.001000
F(0.010000) = 0.009950
F(0.100000) = 0.095163
F(1.000000) = 0.632121
F(2.000000) = 0.864665
F(3.000000) = 0.950213
f(0.000000) = 1.000000
f(0.000100) = 0.999900
f(0.001000) = 0.999000
f(0.010000) = 0.990050
f(0.100000) = 0.904837
f(1.000000) = 0.367879
f(2.000000) = 0.135335
f(3.000000) = 0.049787

### 12.3.14 Empirical Distribution

The probability distributions that we have discussed so far are all model-based parametric distributions. The shapes of those distributions are determined by a few (shape) parameters. Model-based or parametric distributions require a knowledge or an assumption of the underlying statistical nature of the data set or generating process. For example, we may assume that the rate of atomic decay follows exponential distribution and that stock prices follow log-normal distribution. However, it is sometimes difficult to justify such an assumption or even to find a parametric distribution to describe the data.

Empirical distribution, on the other hand, requires no prior knowledge of the statistical nature of the data set. Its shape is entirely determined by the data set itself. They are useful when we cannot justify or fit a parametric distribution reasonably accurate enough. This may be the case when there are not enough samples or there lacks a theoretical underpinning for the data.

Specifically, an empirical cumulative distribution function is a step function that jumps up by ![$$ \frac{1}{n} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq44.png) at each of the *n* data points. Its value at any specified value of the random variable is the fraction of observations of the variable that are less than or equal to the specified value. The empirical distribution function is an estimate of the cumulative distribution function that generates the points in the sample. It converges with probability 1 to that underlying distribution, according to the Glivenko-Cantelli theorem.

Mathematically, let {*X*[1], ..., *X*[*n*]} be independent, identically distributed real random variables with the same cumulative distribution function *F*(*x*). Then the empirical cumulative distribution function is defined as follows:

![$$ {\hat{F}}_n(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{\mathbf{1}}_{X_i\le x} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfu.png)

where **1**[*A*] is the indicator of event *A*. It equals 1 when the condition or event is satisfied. In this case, the condition is *X*[*i*] ≤ *x*. ![$$ {\hat{F}}_n(x) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq45.png) is an unbiased estimator for *F*(*x*).

For example, in Figure [12-41](#500382_1_En_12_Chapter.xhtml#Fig41), the smooth curve, which asymptotically approaches heights of 0 and 1 without reaching them, is the true cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution. The hash marks at the bottom represent the observations in a particular sample drawn from that distribution. The horizontal steps of the step function (including the leftmost point in each step but not including the rightmost point) form the empirical distribution function of that sample.

![../images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig41_HTML.jpg](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Fig41_HTML.jpg)

Figure 12-41

An empirical distribution versus normal distribution

The quantile function of an empirical distribution of sample size *n* is such that if *nq* is not an integer, then the *q*-th quantile is unique and is equal to the ![$$ \overline{nq} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq46.png)-th sample, where ![$$ \overline{nq} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_IEq47.png) is the biggest integer less than or equal to *nq*.

![$$ Q(q)={x}_{\overline{nq}} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfv.png)

If *nq* is an integer, then the *q*-th quantile is not unique and is any real number *x* such that:

![$$ {x}_{nq}&lt;x&lt;{x}_{nq+1} $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfw.png)

The mean is an unbiased estimator of the mean of the population distribution:

![$$ {\mathrm{E}}_n(X)=\overline{x}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{x}_i\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfx.png)

The variance is as follows:

![$$ Var(X)=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum \limits_{i=1}^n{\left({x}_i-\overline{x}\right)}^2\right) $$](images/500382_1_En_12_Chapter/500382_1_En_12_Chapter_TeX_Equfy.png)

The skewness is the sample skewness.

The excess kurtosis is the sample excess kurtosis.

The NM Dev class `EmpiricalDistribution` computes the empirical distribution for a data set. Here’s an example:

```
// the data set
double[] X = new double[]{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 99};
// construct the empirical distribution from the data set
EmpiricalDistribution dist = new EmpiricalDistribution(X);
System.out.println("mean = " + dist.mean());
System.out.println("variance = " + dist.variance());
System.out.println("skew = " + dist.skew());
System.out.println("kurtosis = " + dist.kurtosis());
double[] xs = new double[]{
0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 2, 3};
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("F(%f) = %f", x, dist.cdf(x)));
}
for (double x : xs) {
System.out.println(String.format("f(%f) = %f", x, dist.density(x)));
}
boolean allEquals = true;
for (double u = 0.1; u  1e-9) {
allEquals = false;
}
}
System.out.println("F(Q(u)) = u for all u = " + allEquals);
```

The output is as follows:

```
